posts.credit: Weihao Cheng · arXiv · cs.AI
posts.title: Teaching AI to design games people actually enjoy playing
posts.sub: Games built by AI are often playable but boring, and this work aims to make them genuinely fun.
posts.author: Weihao Cheng
posts.summary: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The problem with AI games","p":["AI agents can now build games that run and can be played. But playable is not the same as engaging. A big part of what keeps people playing is the feeling of steadily getting better at something, a quality known as mastery."]},{"h":"What the team is tackling","p":["Designing a game so players can keep improving usually takes extensive human playtesting and careful tuning. The researchers behind PlayCraft are working on letting an AI agent's own play experience guide that design work, instead of relying only on human trial and error.","The idea is that an agent playing its own game can notice where the challenge feels rewarding and where it feels flat, and use that experience to shape the design."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["If agents can learn what makes a game satisfying from their own attempts, game creation could become faster and cheaper while producing games people actually want to keep playing. This is early-stage research on design methods, not a finished product."]}]}

posts.orig_sub: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning.

posts.title: AI learns how the world moves by reusing video models
posts.sub: Understanding the hidden actions behind video could help robots and AI systems learn from ordinary footage.
posts.author: Yuxin Jiang, Wenqiang Sun, Jiaqi Li, et al.
posts.summary: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Learning from plain video","p":["Videos show how scenes change over time, but they rarely show the actions that caused those changes. Researchers try to recover those hidden actions from the visual changes themselves, an approach called latent action learning, so machines can learn cause and effect."]},{"h":"What the team did","p":["Today these systems often learn how the world works largely from scratch. The team instead repurposed a video generation model, a type of AI already trained on how videos unfold, as a starting point for learning the hidden actions behind visual changes.","The starting model already understands how scenes tend to evolve, so the new system does not have to rediscover those basics while learning what actions drive the changes."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Reusing what video models already know could make it much easier for AI to learn from everyday footage. posts.credit: Yang Meng, Zixin Ding, Robert L. Grossman, et al. · arXiv · cs.LG
posts.title: AI learns to pick only the measurements it really needs
posts.sub: Choosing fewer, smarter measurements could cut costs, waiting times and privacy risks when AI makes decisions.
posts.author: Yang Meng, Zixin Ding, Robert L. Grossman, et al.
posts.summary: Acquiring every feature of an instance is often costly: a measurement can carry a monetary price, a time delay, or a privacy cost. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) addresses this by learning a policy that decides, per instance, which features to acquire under a budget.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The cost of knowing everything","p":["When an AI system makes a decision, gathering every possible piece of information is often expensive. Their approach learns from an all-knowing teacher model that sees every measurement, then teaches a practical version to imitate those choices.","The budget can reflect money, time or privacy, and the policy adapts to each case rather than applying one fixed list of measurements to everyone."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["In settings like healthcare or finance, asking for fewer tests or data points could save money and time while protecting privacy, without giving up much decision quality. posts.title: Robots learn to link many careful moves into one task

posts.summary: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Where robots struggle","p":["Today's robot AI models can perform many individual skills, such as picking up an object. But they still struggle with long tasks that combine moving around and handling things, where timing, skill and precision all have to line up inside one model."]},{"h":"What the team is working on","p":["The researchers report progress on helping robots chain these complex moves together into long sequences of careful movement, rather than treating each skill separately. posts.title: A safer way to check when AI answers can be trusted

posts.summary: Self-consistency certification treats repeated sampling from a language model as sequential evidence accumulation and stops when an anytime-valid e-process crosses a threshold, guaranteeing finite-sample Type I error control by Ville's inequality.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The trust problem","p":["Language models can give different answers to the same question. One common check is to ask repeatedly and see whether the answers agree. But deciding when agreement is strong enough to trust has lacked firm statistical guarantees."]},{"h":"What the team did","p":["The researchers treat repeated answers as evidence that builds up over time, and stop checking once it crosses a set threshold. Their method comes with a mathematical guarantee that limits false alarms, even when only a small number of samples is used.","Because the check can stop at any point while keeping its guarantee, it does not need a fixed number of questions decided in advance, which makes it practical to run."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Tools built on language models are increasingly used for real decisions. A principled way to certify when answers are reliable could help developers know when to trust a model and when to keep checking, making AI-assisted decisions safer."]}]}

posts.credit: Jiahao Huang, Jun Wang · arXiv · cs.AI
posts.title: Researchers probe how AI models combine what they see and read
posts.sub: The study borrows a theory of human consciousness to look inside AI systems that understand images and text.
posts.author: Jiahao Huang, Jun Wang
posts.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Looking inside AI","p":["AI models that handle both images and text can answer questions about what they see, but their answers do not reveal how concepts are represented inside. The researchers wanted a window into that hidden internal structure."]},{"h":"A theory borrowed from brains","p":["They tested ideas from global workspace theory, which proposes that the brain selects information from many parallel processes, combines it in a shared space, and makes it available to specialised processes. The team probed whether similar patterns appear in these AI models.","The probes look for signs that information is selected, combined in a shared space, and then made available to other parts of the model, mirroring the theory's picture of the brain."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Understanding how AI organises information internally could help researchers build more transparent systems. posts.title: AI double-checks chip designs for bugs that tests miss
posts.sub: Some chip design errors pass every test, and a new AI check aims to catch them before production.
posts.author: Ana E. Sanchez Villalobos, Michael D. Quinn, Aakash Tyagi, et al.
posts.summary: A passing UVM regression shows the design agrees with the reference model on what the scoreboard checks, not that it meets the specification. Bugs that pass every test yet violate the specification, termed scoreboard escapes, survive mature testbenches.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The hidden bug problem","p":["Chip designers run huge test suites, but passing them only shows the design matches a reference model on what the tests check. Bugs that satisfy every test yet break the written specification can survive even mature testing setups.","These escapes happen because the reference model and the tests share the same blind spots: anything neither of them checks can pass silently, even in well-tested designs."]},{"h":"What the team built","p":["The researchers use a large language model to cross-check designs directly against the specification, the document describing what the chip must actually do. The idea is to verify the verifier: checking the checks themselves, not just the design."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Chips power phones, cars and medical devices, and fixing a design flaw after manufacturing is enormously costly. posts.credit: Adrià Ciurana Lanau, Harleen Hanspal, Lusine Abrahamyan, et al. · arXiv · cs.AI
posts.title: A leaner way for AI to generate editable layered designs
posts.sub: Graphic designs made of separate layers are easier to edit, and this method represents those layers more compactly.
posts.author: Adrià Ciurana Lanau, Harleen Hanspal, Lusine Abrahamyan, et al.
posts.summary: Graphic designs are ordered compositions of RGBA layers whose separation enables selection, movement, and reuse. Existing layered models represent each layer with a full-canvas or region-sized spatial latent grid, so representation size grows with the cumulative spatial extent of the layers.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Why layers matter","p":["Graphic designs are built from stacked layers, like transparent sheets. Keeping layers separate lets designers select, move and reuse each element. AI tools that generate designs want to preserve that structure so the results stay editable."]},{"h":"What the team changed","p":["Existing AI models store each layer as a grid covering the whole canvas or a region, so the storage grows with the layers' size. ProtoDiffusion instead represents each layer with a compact set of tokens, one group per layer, keeping the representation small.","Because each layer gets its own compact token group, the size of the representation no longer balloons with the area the layers cover on the canvas."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["A smaller representation could make layered design generation faster and lighter to run, while keeping designs fully editable. This is early-stage research on how AI represents images, not a finished design product you can buy today."]}]}

posts.sub: Careful reasoning improves AI answers but is slow, and this method aims to keep the quality without the wait.
posts.author: Sahibzada Allahyar, Julia White, Dhruv Atreja, et al.
posts.summary: Decision models enable fast, confidence-aware decisions by scoring candidate answers in a single forward pass, without generating text or intermediate reasoning. Yet reasoning can substantially improve decision quality, raising the question of whether its benefits can be retained without the cost of generating it.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Speed versus thought","p":["Letting an AI model think step by step improves its decisions, but generating all that reasoning is slow and costly. posts.title: AI guides that know when to speak and when to stay quiet

posts.summary: Real-time task guidance is inherently flexible: when an agent guides a user through a task, multiple responses and timings can be appropriate, and sometimes the best action is to remain silent.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Guidance is more than answers","p":["When an AI assistant guides someone through a real task, several responses and timings can be appropriate. Silence becomes a deliberate, useful option, not a failure to answer at all."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Assistants that interrupt at the wrong time are annoying or worse. posts.title: A new training rule steers AI toward more stable solutions
posts.sub: How AI models are trained affects how robust they are, and this rule comes with mathematical guarantees.
posts.author: Francesco Caporali, Jason M. Altschuler, Boris Hanin
posts.summary: We present a new adaptive stepsize rule that biases gradient descent toward flatter minima in both theory and practice, and establish the first uniform-in-time guarantees for both sharpness and loss reduction for a broad class of locally quadratic objectives.

The size of each adjustment matters: some settings lead to fragile solutions, while flatter, more forgiving ones tend to behave better on new data.","Think of it as choosing how boldly to adjust the model at each step. Too bold and training lands in sharp, brittle spots; the new rule aims for gentler, flatter ground."]},{"h":"What the team proved","p":["The researchers present a new adaptive rule for choosing these adjustment sizes, designed to steer training toward flatter solutions. They also established the first guarantees of their kind showing the rule controls both stability and error reduction over time."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Training choices shape how reliable AI models are in the real world. posts.summary: Does post-training change what a language model represents, or how this representation is read out into an answer? We compared linear probes with the models' own answers, analyzed with signal detection theory, in six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"A question about training","p":["After their initial training, language models get further tuning to make them helpful. posts.credit: Ambroise Borbely, Mathieu Salzmann, Olivier Verscheure · arXiv · cs.LG
posts.title: AI language models may not need every calculation
posts.sub: Researchers are testing whether AI chatbots can skip some internal math and still give good answers.
posts.author: Ambroise Borbely, Mathieu Salzmann, Olivier Verscheure
posts.summary: Attention in large language models (LLMs) scores every query against every key with a full dot product. We investigate whether this dot product must be computed completely for attention to be effective.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"What the team asked","p":["When a language model reads your message, it compares every word with every other word to decide what matters. Each comparison uses a full calculation. It is one of the most expensive steps in how these systems work. The researchers asked whether all of that work is really needed."]},{"h":"What they tried","p":["The team tested a method called HiSA that leaves out parts of these comparisons. The goal was to see whether the model can pay attention to the right words while doing less math. The question sounds small, but it touches the core of how these models understand language."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["These comparisons are a big part of the work behind AI chatbots. If some steps can be safely skipped, future models could become cheaper to run. This is early-stage research, not a finished product, and the team is exploring how far the shortcut can go."]}]}

posts.credit: Ilya Gusev · arXiv · cs.CL
posts.title: Peer reviews are growing more alike in the AI era
posts.sub: Science relies on reviewers spotting different problems, but measurements show their critiques are increasingly overlapping.
posts.author: Ilya Gusev
posts.summary: Peer review relies on several readers finding different problems. We measure critique overlap in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR, measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage of the review process, with year-on-year rises at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Why variety matters","p":["Peer review works because several readers find different problems in a paper. If reviewers start saying the same things, weaknesses can slip through unnoticed and the quality filter of science gets weaker."]},{"h":"What the team measured","p":["The researcher measured how much critiques overlap in conference and journal reviews. At one major AI conference, overlap rose from 12.0 percent in 2026 to 21.3 percent in 2027, with year-on-year rises at other major venues too.","The comparisons used reviews from the same stage of the review process, so the measured rise is not simply an artefact of comparing early drafts with final versions of reviews. That makes the trend harder to dismiss."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["The pattern coincides with the spread of AI writing tools, though the study measures overlap rather than proving its cause. posts.credit: Marc Jansen · arXiv · cs.CL
posts.title: Researchers ask if AI can be taught new ways of thinking
posts.sub: Step-by-step reasoning helped AI models, and this work explores whether their inner thinking style can be deliberately changed.
posts.author: Marc Jansen
posts.summary: Reasoning capabilities in large language models have evolved from prompting-based methods to internalized model behaviors. In this paper, we investigate whether the internal thinking model of an LLM can be deliberately changed and whether such a change is beneficial.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Beyond step-by-step","p":["Language models got better at reasoning first through prompts asking them to think step by step, and later through thinking behaviours built into the models themselves. posts.credit: Handa Li, Pengxiang Li, Mingyu Cao, et al. · arXiv · cs.CL
posts.title: A looping trick to make text-generating AI faster
posts.sub: Some AI writes whole sentences at once but needs many refinement rounds, and this method aims to cut them.
posts.author: Handa Li, Pengxiang Li, Mingyu Cao, et al.
posts.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) support parallel generation, yet they often require many denoising steps because only a fraction of token predictions are sufficiently reliable to be committed at each step. Existing acceleration methods primarily optimize confidence learning or commitment policies.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Parallel writing, slow finishing","p":["Diffusion language models generate text in parallel rather than word by word. But at each refinement step only some predictions are reliable enough to keep, so many steps are needed before the text is finished."]},{"h":"What the team built","p":["dLoop adds a looping refinement process inside the model, reworking its internal representations repeatedly so more predictions become reliable sooner. Earlier speed-up methods mostly tuned confidence estimates or which predictions to commit at each step.","The loop refines the model's internal state repeatedly before predictions are committed, rather than only adjusting how confidence is estimated. More reliable predictions per step means fewer steps overall to finish the text. That is where the speed comes from."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Fewer refinement steps could make this style of text generation noticeably faster and cheaper to run. It is early-stage research, and real-world gains depend on further testing across different tasks."]}]}

posts.title: New method stops sample shifts from faking cell movement
posts.sub: Truer maps of how cells change over time and space could sharpen studies of development and disease.

posts.summary: Learning the spatiotemporal dynamics of cells from spatial transcriptomics requires connecting snapshots of different cells acquired in different coordinate frames. A rotation or translation of a section can appear as cell movement and distort the inferred correspondence.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The problem","p":["To learn how cells move and change, researchers connect snapshots of tissue taken at different times. But each snapshot sits in its own coordinate frame: a rotated or shifted section can look like cell movement that never happened."]},{"h":"What the team built","p":["Their method, horizontal flow matching, connects snapshots while accounting for these frame differences, so that genuine cell dynamics are separated from mere shifts of the sample. posts.credit: Zihan Wang, Jianzhe Li, Zhenyi Zhang, et al. · arXiv · cs.LG
posts.title: New tool traces how cell populations change from snapshots
posts.sub: It could help scientists study how tissues grow and renew without tracking individual cells over time.
posts.author: Zihan Wang, Jianzhe Li, Zhenyi Zhang, et al.
posts.summary: Reconstructing cellular dynamics from snapshots is challenging because the destructive nature of single-cell measurements makes tracking the same cells over time impossible. Cellular dynamics are inherently stochastic and involve changes in population size through proliferation and apoptosis.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The problem","p":["Measuring a single cell in detail usually destroys it, so scientists cannot follow the same cells over time. Instead they collect snapshots of different cells at different moments, and must piece together the story of how the population changed."]},{"h":"What the team built","p":["The researchers developed Elysium, a mathematical method that reconstructs cell dynamics directly from these snapshots. It handles two realities of living tissue: cells behave randomly, and the population itself grows or shrinks as cells divide and die. It needs no costly simulations.","Because each measurement destroys the cell it reads, every snapshot shows different individuals. The method must therefore infer two things at once: the random paths cells take between snapshots, and how the population's size changes as cells divide and die."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["This is early-stage method work, not a finished product. But it could help biologists study how tissues develop, renew themselves or respond to treatment, using the kind of snapshot data labs already collect every day."]}]}

posts.credit: Ting Long, Xiaojing Sun, Cheng Han, et al. · arXiv · cs.CV
posts.title: A new model predicts how single cells change after gene edits
posts.sub: It forecasts both how a cell will look and when it will divide after a gene is switched off.
posts.author: Ting Long, Xiaojing Sun, Cheng Han, et al.
posts.summary: A cell observed after a gene knockdown has an uncertain future, both in how its appearance will evolve and when it will divide. Existing approaches predict endpoints or population-level changes without jointly modeling individual trajectories and division timing.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The question","p":["When scientists switch off a gene in a cell, the cell's future becomes uncertain. Its appearance changes in unpredictable ways, and no one knows exactly when it will next divide. Understanding this matters for studying what genes actually do."]},{"h":"What the team built","p":["The team created MitoWorld, a computer model of the single-cell life cycle. Unlike earlier approaches that predict only final outcomes or average population changes, it models each cell's individual journey and its division timing together, including the randomness involved.","The model treats the cell's future as genuinely uncertain. It describes the range of ways a cell's appearance might evolve and the possible moments when it might divide, rather than committing to a single fixed prediction for every cell."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["This is early-stage modelling work in the lab. If it holds up, researchers could better predict how genetic changes ripple through growing cell populations, helping them interpret experiments that switch genes off."]}]}

posts.orig_sub: A cell observed after a gene knockdown has an uncertain future, both in how its appearance will evolve and when it will divide. Existing approaches predict endpoints or population-level changes without jointly modeling individual trajectories and division timing.

posts.summary: Accurately predicting a small molecule's binding affinity to a protein, a critical task in drug discovery, remains challenging. Physics-based approaches like free-energy perturbation (FEP) have very high computational costs and require expert setup.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"A key drug-discovery step","p":["Before a molecule can become a medicine, it usually has to grip a target protein tightly. posts.summary: Background: Quantifying myocardial strains from Displacement ENcoding with Stimulated Echoes (DENSE) MRI provides insight into left ventricular performance, but current data processing pipelines remain limited in automation, robustness, and full left ventricle coverage.

Some of the information the detector worked hard to capture never reaches the final image, and this model aims to keep it."]},{"h":"What the team built","p":["The researchers developed SPLAT, a model of the scanner's response that treats each event individually with its full detail, rather than sorting detections into coarse bins. posts.credit: Konstantinos Dovelos · arXiv · cs.CE
posts.title: A checking system verifies simulations of heart ablation therapy
posts.sub: As software increasingly predicts heart treatment outcomes unattended, this work adds mathematical guarantees to the results.
posts.author: Konstantinos Dovelos
posts.summary: Computational models of pulsed field ablation predict the lesion as the tissue where the electric field exceeds a lethal threshold. Their numerical error is rarely bounded, and automated pipelines increasingly run them without an expert checking each result.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Trusting the simulation","p":["Pulsed field ablation is a heart treatment that uses electric pulses to disable tissue causing rhythm problems. Computer models predict which tissue the pulses will affect, and automated pipelines increasingly run these models without an expert checking each result.","The models mark tissue as treated wherever the predicted electric field crosses a lethal threshold. Errors in the computed field therefore translate directly into errors in the predicted treatment zone, which is why bounded error matters. Unchecked models carry real risk."]},{"h":"What the team did","p":["The researcher developed a certificate-based verification approach that bounds the numerical error of these simulations. Instead of trusting the computed prediction blindly, the method produces a checkable guarantee about its accuracy."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["As treatment planning becomes more automated, knowing a simulation's error is bounded could make its predictions safer to rely on. posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Slow, expert-only calculations","p":["Predicting how a material's atoms settle into place, and how its electrons behave, normally takes heavy computation and deep specialist knowledge. These first-principles calculations are a workhorse of materials research, but their cost and complexity keep them out of many hands. They are essential for designing new materials."]},{"h":"What the team built","p":["The researchers present Perfumer, a system built around a large language model that acts as an automated assistant. It connects an established simulation package with two predictive models, steering the calculations so structures and electronic properties can be worked out with less manual effort."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["If the assistant proves reliable, it could shorten the wait for computational results and lower the expertise barrier, helping teams screen and understand new materials more quickly. The calculations it automates normally demand both serious computer time and specialist skill. It is a research framework, not yet a turnkey product."]}]}

posts.credit: Jacqueline Hidalgo-Jiménez, Payam Edalati, Md Amirul Islam, et al. · arXiv · cond-mat.mtrl-sci
posts.title: Heavily deformed metal alloy conducts heat and power better
posts.sub: An unusual finding could change how engineers tune alloys for electronics and cooling.
posts.author: Jacqueline Hidalgo-Jiménez, Payam Edalati, Md Amirul Islam, et al.
posts.summary: This work investigates how defect engineering and nanostructuring via severe plastic deformation influence electrical and thermal transport in the high-entropy alloy CrMnFeCoNi.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"A surprise in a tough alloy","p":["CrMnFeCoNi is a high-entropy alloy, a metal built from five elements mixed in near-equal amounts, prized for its toughness. Normally, hammering or squeezing a metal until its internal structure is heavily disrupted makes it worse at carrying electricity and heat. The alloy mixes chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt and nickel."]},{"h":"What the team found","p":["The researchers severely deformed this alloy, creating a dense web of defects and extremely fine internal grains. Unexpectedly, its electrical and thermal conductivity increased rather than fell. They examined how this defect engineering and nanostructuring changed the way charge and heat move through the metal."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["The result goes against the usual rule of thumb for worked metals, suggesting deformation could become a tool for tuning how alloys handle current and heat. That could matter for durable components that must also manage warmth in demanding settings. The effect was measured for both electricity and heat."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Unusual increase in electrical and thermal conductivity of severely deformed CrMnFeCoNi
posts.orig_sub: This work investigates how defect engineering and nanostructuring via severe plastic deformation influence electrical and thermal transport in the high-entropy alloy CrMnFeCoNi.

posts.credit: Ryotaro Okabe, Shoki Kishida, Abhijatmedhi Chotrattanapituk, et al. · arXiv · cond-mat.mtrl-sci
posts.title: When AI scores disagree with experts, new materials may hide
posts.sub: Disagreements between an AI's scoring rules and human judgment might point to overlooked materials.
posts.author: Ryotaro Okabe, Shoki Kishida, Abhijatmedhi Chotrattanapituk, et al.
posts.summary: Reward misalignment is usually regarded as a failure of artificial intelligence. In materials discovery with generative AI models, however, disagreement between predefined rewards and expert judgment may reveal materials that the rewards overlook.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Usually seen as a flaw","p":["AI systems are often trained to chase a numerical score, and when their choices stop matching that score, engineers usually treat it as a failure to fix. The score stands in for what researchers actually want. In materials discovery, generative AI proposes candidate materials judged by such predefined scores."]},{"h":"A different way to look","p":["The authors argue that a mismatch between the score and expert judgment can be informative rather than broken. When specialists rate a material highly that the scoring rules rank poorly, the disagreement may flag promising candidates the rules simply overlook. The mismatch itself becomes the signal."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Treating these mismatches as clues rather than errors could widen the search for useful materials, catching candidates a rigid score would discard. Expert judgment becomes a resource, not just a check. The idea reframes a common AI problem as a discovery opportunity worth exploring."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Reward misalignment as an opportunity for materials discovery
posts.orig_sub: Reward misalignment is usually regarded as a failure of artificial intelligence. In materials discovery with generative AI models, however, disagreement between predefined rewards and expert judgment may reveal materials that the rewards overlook.

posts.credit: Asmund Ottesen, Shun Feng, Edoardo Lopriore, et al. · arXiv · cond-mat.mes-hall
posts.title: Sliding atomic layers steers light particles in a crystal
posts.sub: Electrically controlling these light-linked particles could help build new light-based electronic devices.
posts.author: Asmund Ottesen, Shun Feng, Edoardo Lopriore, et al.
posts.summary: A fundamental property of interlayer excitons is their dipolar character, enabling electrical tunability, enhanced exciton-exciton interactions and extended lifetime. It is important for studying collective phenomena and realizing novel optoelectronic devices.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Particles made of light","p":["When light is absorbed in a thin crystal, it can create an exciton, a paired electron and hole that carries energy. In stacked two-layer materials these pairs can act like tiny electric dipoles, which makes them tunable with voltage and longer-lived. Their behaviour is central to how such materials interact with light."]},{"h":"What the team showed","p":["Working with stacked layers of tungsten diselenide, the researchers used a sliding effect between the layers, which flips the stack's internal electric polarization, to control two kinds of these excitons. The sliding gives an electrical handle on how the pairs behave."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Controllable, long-lived excitons are interesting both for studying how many such particles act together and for future devices that process information with light. This is early-stage physics, but it adds a useful control knob for layered materials. The control works without any change to the material's chemistry."]}]}

posts.credit: DaVonne Henry, Dominick S. Scaletta, Tamar M. Padwa, et al. · arXiv · cond-mat.mes-hall
posts.title: New self-check for the quantum devices that define resistance
posts.sub: More reliable electrical standards would underpin the precise measurements modern technology depends on.
posts.author: DaVonne Henry, Dominick S. Scaletta, Tamar M. Padwa, et al.
posts.summary: The scaling of multi-element quantized Hall array resistance standards necessitates rigorous validation that internal quantization has not broken down without relying on the verification of dissipationless edge state transport.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The ruler for resistance","p":["Laboratories around the world rely on quantum devices whose electrical resistance takes an exact, unchanging value set by nature. These quantum Hall standards anchor electrical measurement, and combining many elements into arrays lets them cover more useful resistance values. The value is fixed by fundamental constants, not by manufacturing."]},{"h":"What the team developed","p":["Bigger arrays raise a worry: one element might quietly lose its perfect quantization. The researchers describe a way for such a standard to verify itself, using the robust physics of the quantum Hall effect, without needing separate checks of the currents flowing along the device's edges."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["A standard that can confirm its own accuracy makes larger, more versatile resistance references more trustworthy, and self-verification becomes more valuable as arrays grow. That strengthens the measurement chain behind calibrating instruments, from laboratory equipment to everyday electronics. The work remains at the research stage."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Topology-Enabled Self-Verification of Quantum Hall Resistance Standards
posts.orig_sub: The scaling of multi-element quantized Hall array resistance standards necessitates rigorous validation that internal quantization has not broken down without relying on the verification of dissipationless edge state transport.

posts.credit: Saurav Patel, Meet Shah, Prafulla K. Jha · arXiv · cond-mat.mtrl-sci
posts.title: Theory predicts unusual electron states in handed crystals
posts.sub: The work maps how the shape of electron waves could produce measurable new effects.
posts.author: Saurav Patel, Meet Shah, Prafulla K. Jha
posts.summary: Quantum geometry of Bloch wave functions and crystalline symmetries play a central role in condensed matter physics, shaping the electronic topology and physical responses of solids.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Geometry inside crystals","p":["Electrons in a solid behave like waves, and the subtle geometry of those waves, together with the crystal's symmetry, shapes many of a material's electrical and magnetic responses. Certain crystals with a built-in handedness can host especially unusual electron states. These responses underpin many of the quantum materials being explored today."]},{"h":"What the theory predicts","p":["The authors study exotic electron states that carry a multiplied topological charge, a kind of mathematical label that makes them robust. They work out how these states should show up in electrical responses and in the oscillations a material displays under strong magnetic fields."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["The predictions give experimentalists concrete signatures to hunt for in real crystals using standard laboratory measurements. Confirming them would deepen the understanding of how quantum geometry turns ordinary-looking materials into hosts for exotic, potentially useful electron behaviour. The work is theoretical and awaits experimental confirmation."]}]}

posts.credit: Aljoscha Felix Baumann, Reyhaneh Ghassemizadeh, Daniel F. Urban · arXiv · cond-mat.mtrl-sci
posts.title: Study examines how added metals affect nickel alloy seams
posts.sub: The tiny internal boundaries in metals help decide whether a part holds together or cracks.
posts.author: Aljoscha Felix Baumann, Reyhaneh Ghassemizadeh, Daniel F. Urban
posts.summary: Grain boundaries (GBs) in polycrystalline Ni-based alloys strongly influence mechanical strength and fracture behavior, yet the effect of alloying elements such as Fe and Cr on GB cohesion remains difficult to quantify systematically.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Where metals fail","p":["Metal parts are made of many tiny crystals pressed together, and the seams between them, called grain boundaries, strongly influence strength and cracking. A weak seam can let a crack spread through the whole part. In nickel-based alloys, how added iron and chromium change these seams has been hard to pin down."]},{"h":"What the team did","p":["The researchers systematically studied the nickel-iron-chromium system, examining how varying the recipe of alloying elements changes the cohesion of grain boundaries, the internal glue holding the crystals together. Their work aims to quantify effects that were previously difficult to compare."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Knowing which additions toughen the seams and which weaken them gives engineers a rational basis for designing longer-lasting alloys. Better predictions of where cracks start could improve the reliability of components that face heat and stress. The work is computational materials science, aimed at guiding better alloy design."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Alloying effects on the interface cohesion of grain boundaries in the Ni--Fe--Cr system
posts.orig_sub: Grain boundaries (GBs) in polycrystalline Ni-based alloys strongly influence mechanical strength and fracture behavior, yet the effect of alloying elements such as Fe and Cr on GB cohesion remains difficult to quantify systematically.

posts.title: Hair-thin alloy wires studied for their large shape change
posts.sub: Wires that change length with temperature could become tiny moving parts in future devices.

posts.summary: The martensitic transformation and associated tensile strain of \mathrm{Ni}_{50}\mathrm{Fe}_{23}\mathrm{Ga}_{27} microwires produced by the Taylor--Ulitovsky method were investigated using thermomechanical analysis, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and in-situ tensile X-ray diffraction (XRD).
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Wires that change shape","p":["Some alloys undergo a solid-to-solid rearrangement of their atoms when conditions change, and the shift can make the material noticeably longer or shorter. Researchers are exploring this effect in extremely fine wires of nickel, iron and gallium, drawn using a special glass-coating technique."]},{"h":"What the team measured","p":["The team tracked the transformation and the stretching it produces in these microwires using thermal and mechanical analysis, detailed imaging of the crystal grains, and X-ray measurements taken while the wires were pulled. Together the methods reveal how the internal structure and the large length change are linked."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["A large, controllable length change in a hair-thin wire is attractive for miniature devices that need tiny, precise movements, such as small robots or medical tools. posts.credit: Ramasamy Murugesan, Shiyu Deng, Marie-Bernadette Lepetit · arXiv · cond-mat.mtrl-sci
posts.title: Simulations map magnetism in a family of nickel oxide films
posts.sub: The calculations explore how atom choice and the underlying surface tune magnetism in thin films.
posts.author: Ramasamy Murugesan, Shiyu Deng, Marie-Bernadette Lepetit
posts.summary: In this paper we present a systematic first-principles investigation of the structure and nearest-neighbor magnetic exchange interactions in the infinite-layer RNiO2 thin-film series (R = La-Lu), under the constrain of different substrates.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"A tunable magnetic family","p":["Thin films of nickel oxides can be grown with different rare-earth atoms tucked into their structure, from lanthanum to lutetium. Each choice changes the spacing of the atoms, and growing the film on different underlying surfaces squeezes or stretches it further. The films are grown on supporting crystal surfaces."]},{"h":"What the team calculated","p":["Using first-principles simulations, calculations built directly on quantum physics rather than fitted parameters, the researchers systematically worked out the structure and the magnetic interactions between neighbouring atoms across the whole series. They examined how the rare-earth atom's size and the strain from the substrate shape those interactions."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["The results give a map of how two practical knobs, chemical choice and substrate strain, control magnetism in this material family. The study covers the full series of rare-earth choices and several substrates. That guidance helps experimental teams design films with the magnetic behaviour they want."]}]}

posts.title: New software helps read movies of electrons inside materials
posts.sub: A shared analysis tool could make advanced electron-imaging experiments easier to interpret.
posts.author: Paul Werner, Wiebke Bennecke, Jan Philipp Bange, et al.
posts.summary: Photoemission momentum microscopy is an emerging approach to photoelectron spectroscopy that is transforming electronic band structure mapping at both laboratory-based and large-scale facilities.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Filming electrons at work","p":["A technique called momentum microscopy knocks electrons out of a material with light and records where they go, revealing the energy patterns that govern how a material conducts. Adding ultrafast laser pulses lets researchers follow these patterns as they change moment by moment."]},{"h":"What the team released","p":["The authors present momipy, a structured software workflow for analysing these time-resolved measurements. It guides the raw, complex data through the steps needed to produce clear maps of electron behaviour, supporting experiments at both ordinary laboratories and large research facilities. The software packages the analysis steps into a single, repeatable workflow."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["As this imaging method spreads, a common analysis pipeline makes results easier to reproduce and compare between groups. The workflow is designed for the growing community using this technique. That lowers the effort needed to turn demanding measurements into insight about materials for future electronics."]}]}

posts.title: Precision experiment tests the tiny forces of empty space
posts.sub: Settling a puzzle about these forces matters for the tiny machines of the future.
posts.author: M. Dhital, G. L. Klimchitskaya, V. M. Mostepanenko, et al.
posts.summary: We report a high-precision experiment on measuring the low-frequency magnetic field reflected from a metallic plate. This experiment is designed to give insight into why theoretical predictions of the fundamental Lifshitz theory using the standard response function to the electromagnetic waves are in contradiction
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Forces from nothing","p":["Even empty space is alive with fleeting electromagnetic fluctuations, and they push on nearby objects with a tiny force. The effect is small but real, and it grows as objects get closer. At the scale of nanotechnology these quantum vacuum forces become significant, so engineers need reliable predictions."]},{"h":"What the team measured","p":["The researchers performed a high-precision experiment measuring how a low-frequency magnetic field reflects from a metal plate. The setup probes a known disagreement between measurements and the standard physics of tiny forces, aiming to pinpoint where the usual description of the metal's response goes wrong. The measurement is designed to isolate the source of the disagreement."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Resolving the mismatch would sharpen the theory engineers rely on when designing nanoscale devices, where unexpected forces can make parts stick or misbehave. posts.credit: O. I. Kushnerov · arXiv · cond-mat.mtrl-sci
posts.title: Simulations watch a five-metal alloy freeze into nanowires
posts.sub: Watching alloys solidify atom by atom could guide how tiny metal wires are made.
posts.author: O. I. Kushnerov
posts.summary: Molecular dynamics simulation of the solidification behavior of an AlCoCuFeNi high-entropy alloy nanowire was performed using an embedded atom model potential at cooling rates of 10^11, 10^12, and 10^13 K/s. Periodic boundary conditions were applied along the nanowire axis to model an effectively infinite nanowire.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Freezing metal, atom by atom","p":["High-entropy alloys blend five or more metals in near-equal amounts and can have unusual properties. How such an alloy turns from liquid to solid matters, because the freezing process sets the internal structure that determines how the finished material behaves. Nanowires are wires only a handful of atoms across."]},{"h":"What the team simulated","p":["Using atom-by-atom computer simulations, the researcher followed the solidification of an aluminium-cobalt-copper-iron-nickel alloy nanowire, a wire only atoms wide. Three different, extremely fast cooling rates were compared, and the wire was treated as effectively endless along its length to focus on the freezing itself. The model tracks every atom's motion."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Cooling speed is one of the few knobs manufacturers can turn when making tiny wires. The simulations reveal how the atoms arrange themselves as the wire freezes, giving a rational basis for choosing processing conditions, though this is simulation work awaiting experimental confirmation."]}]}

posts.credit: Kristina Holsgrove, Ronan Lynch, Conor McCluskey, et al. · arXiv · cond-mat.mes-hall
posts.title: Twisted crystals reveal tiny spiral structures at their seam
posts.sub: The unexpected spirals could become new building blocks for future electronic devices.
posts.author: Kristina Holsgrove, Ronan Lynch, Conor McCluskey, et al.
posts.summary: We report that twisted interfaces, formed between two ferroelectric lithium niobate single crystals, contain arrays of coherently bonded and elastically deformed nanoscale structural helices, separated from one another by screw dislocations.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Twisting two crystals together","p":["Lithium niobate is a crystal widely used in optics and electronics, with a built-in electric polarization. When two such crystals are bonded together with a twist between their atomic patterns, the interface must accommodate the mismatch, and interesting structures can emerge there."]},{"h":"What the team found","p":["The researchers report that these twisted interfaces contain arrays of nanoscale helices, tiny spiral distortions of the atomic structure that remain firmly bonded to the surrounding crystal. Each helix is only nanometres across, elastically strained and separated from its neighbours by line defects where the atomic planes step like a spiral staircase."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Finding ordered structures hidden inside a familiar material opens a new design space. The spirals form spontaneously at the bonded interface rather than being carved. The authors suggest these helices could serve as building blocks for next-generation electronics, an idea that now needs further exploration."]}]}

posts.title: AI-assisted imaging maps heat flow in tiny structures
posts.sub: Seeing exactly how heat moves could improve chips, materials and advanced manufacturing.
posts.author: Xin Qian, Te-Huan Liu, Xiaobo Li, et al.
posts.summary: The ability to measure thermal properties and visualize heat transport processes with high spatial resolution is becoming increasingly important for materials discovery, next-generation electronics, and advanced manufacturing.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Heat at the smallest scales","p":["As devices shrink, managing heat becomes harder: hot spots only nanometres across can limit performance or damage components. Traditional tools struggle to see heat at this scale. Measuring thermal properties and watching heat move in fine detail is increasingly important for materials discovery, electronics and manufacturing."]},{"h":"What the work covers","p":["The authors describe intelligent imaging approaches that combine sensitive thermal measurement techniques with AI-based analysis. The goal is to turn complex signals into clear pictures of how heat travels through nanostructures, faster and with more detail than manual interpretation allows. The authors survey how AI can sharpen these thermal measurements."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Better heat maps would let engineers spot problems and test new materials more quickly, from next-generation chips to advanced manufacturing processes. The work points toward smarter tools for materials discovery rather than reporting a single finished instrument. The payoff is faster, clearer insight into heat at the nanoscale."]}]}

posts.credit: Ganesh Hanchanahal, Arnav Jain, Shrushti Tapar, et al. · arXiv · cond-mat.mes-hall
posts.title: A single atomic layer switches magnets without a field
posts.sub: Removing the need for an external magnet brings a promising type of computer memory closer.
posts.author: Ganesh Hanchanahal, Arnav Jain, Shrushti Tapar, et al.
posts.summary: An important step towards the practical implementation of spin-orbit torque magnetic memory is the field-free switching of the magnetization vector. In this work, we investigate spin-orbit torque-driven magnetization dynamics and switching devices comprising monolayer \mathrm{WTe}_2 as the spin-source material.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"A new kind of memory","p":["Magnetic memory stores bits as the direction of tiny magnets, and switching them with electrical currents rather than magnetic fields could make memory faster and more efficient. The effect used is called spin-orbit torque. One obstacle has been that reliable switching usually still needs an assisting magnetic field."]},{"h":"What the team showed","p":["The researchers built switching devices using a single atomic layer of tungsten ditelluride as the source of the switching effect. They studied how the magnetization moves and demonstrate deterministic, field-free switching, meaning the magnet reliably ends up in the intended direction without any external field."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Field-free operation removes a major practical hurdle for this memory technology, and the switching is driven purely by electrical currents in the device. Using a material just one atom thick hints at very compact devices. The work is an early device demonstration, not a product."]}]}

posts.credit: J. Lukes, D. S. Gaur, V. Kanclir, et al. · arXiv · physics.optics
posts.title: A laser method reveals hidden stress in optical thin films
posts.sub: More sensitive checks of the coatings in lenses and lasers could improve their reliability.
posts.author: J. Lukes, D. S. Gaur, V. Kanclir, et al.
posts.summary: Increasing demands on the performance and reliability of optical thin films stimulate the development of more sensitive characterisation methods capable of investigating thin-film interfaces or local mechanical stress.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Coatings under pressure","p":["Optical devices rely on stacks of thin films, coatings only millionths of a metre thick. Even tiny flaws can scatter light or start damage. As demands on performance grow, weak points at the interfaces between layers, or small pockets of mechanical stress, become harder to find with conventional inspection."]},{"h":"What the team developed","p":["The researchers use a laser technique in which light hitting the material comes back partly at double its original frequency, a signal that is especially sensitive to interfaces. By measuring this signal at different angles, they can probe thin films, their boundaries and local stress."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["A more sensitive way to inspect coatings could catch flaws before they cause failures in lasers, lenses and other precision optics. The technique reads interfaces that ordinary inspection can miss. That supports the push toward more reliable optical components, though the method is still being developed."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Probing thin films and their interfaces via angle-resolved second-harmonic generation
