posts.credit: Zhuokai Xu, Xiaohui Yang, Zhefeng Lou, et al. · arXiv · cond-mat.mtrl-sci
posts.title: Heat makes atomic layers slide in sudden, jerky shifts
posts.sub: Understanding these shifts could help control layered materials used in future devices.
posts.author: Zhuokai Xu, Xiaohui Yang, Zhefeng Lou, et al.
posts.summary: Interlayer sliding in van der Waals materials offers a promising route to control functional properties, yet a comprehensive understanding of the complex collective domain dynamics governing these transitions remains challenging.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Layers that slip","p":["Some crystals are stacks of atomically thin sheets held together by weak forces, and the sheets can slide over one another. Each arrangement of the sheets gives the material different properties, so sliding offers a promising way to switch functionality. But the collective motion of many regions at once is poorly understood."]},{"h":"What the team observed","p":["Studying a layered compound containing lead and tantalum selenide, the researchers found that changing temperature drives the material through several distinct sliding states. The transitions do not happen smoothly: regions rearrange in sudden avalanches, with many domains shifting together in bursts."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Mapping these states and their jerky dynamics is a step toward deliberately controlling sliding-based switching in layered materials. That could inform future devices that store or process information by shifting atomic layers rather than moving charge. The study maps several distinct sliding states within a single material system."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Thermally driven multiple sliding states and avalanche dynamics in rhombohedral Pb(TaSe2)2
posts.orig_sub: Interlayer sliding in van der Waals materials offers a promising route to control functional properties, yet a comprehensive understanding of the complex collective domain dynamics governing these transitions remains challenging.

posts.credit: Xuanyu Zhu, Qian Tan, Bo Chen, et al. · arXiv · cs.AI
posts.title: A general-purpose AI model built for materials science
posts.sub: One AI system that reads text, structures and images could speed up materials research.
posts.author: Xuanyu Zhu, Qian Tan, Bo Chen, et al.
posts.summary: Materials science involves highly heterogeneous scientific information, including textual knowledge, molecular and crystal structures, experimental characterization data, microscopy images, and structure-property relationships.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Scattered knowledge","p":["Materials science runs on many kinds of information at once: written knowledge, molecular and crystal structures, measurement data, microscope images, and the links between a material's structure and its properties. Most AI tools handle only one of these formats at a time, and connecting them by hand is slow."]},{"h":"What the team built","p":["The researchers introduce MatVerse, a foundation model designed for materials science, meaning a broadly trained AI system meant to work across this mixed information. The aim is a single model that can connect text, structures, images and data instead of treating them separately. The system is presented as a research platform."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["A model fluent in all the field's data types could help researchers search, connect and predict across sources that today sit apart. The model is meant as a shared starting point for many tasks. Its real value will be judged by how it performs on practical problems."]}]}
posts.orig_title: MatVerse: A Foundation Model for Materials Science
posts.orig_sub: Materials science involves highly heterogeneous scientific information, including textual knowledge, molecular and crystal structures, experimental characterization data, microscopy images, and structure-property relationships.

posts.credit: Changzhi Ai, Frank Abild-Pedersen, Johannes Voss · arXiv · cond-mat.mtrl-sci
posts.title: A faster AI tool predicts how molecules stick to catalysts
posts.sub: Quickly judging catalyst surfaces could speed the search for cleaner chemical processes.
posts.author: Changzhi Ai, Frank Abild-Pedersen, Johannes Voss
posts.summary: Fast and accurate prediction of adsorption energies is critical for high-throughput computational catalyst screening, existing methods compromise either on evaluation speed (full-graph machine learning potentials) or geometric sensitivity (coordination-based models like the alpha-scheme).
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The catalyst screening problem","p":["Catalysts speed up chemical reactions, and how strongly molecules stick to their surfaces is a key clue to how well they work. This sticking strength is called the adsorption energy. Screening thousands of candidate surfaces by computer requires predicting it quickly and accurately, and existing methods trade one for the other."]},{"h":"What the team built","p":["The researchers present AdsNet, a neural network that treats a surface and its attached molecules as a graph of connected atoms. It predicts adsorption energies directly, aiming to keep the speed needed for large screenings while staying sensitive to the exact geometry of each site."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Faster, geometry-aware predictions could let researchers sift vast numbers of catalyst candidates and focus experiments on the most promising ones. The tool is aimed at large-scale computational screening. That may shorten the path to better catalysts for industry and cleaner chemistry. The network is a research tool."]}]}
posts.orig_title: AdsNet: A Graph Neural Network for Direct Adsorption Energy Prediction
posts.orig_sub: Fast and accurate prediction of adsorption energies is critical for high-throughput computational catalyst screening, existing methods compromise either on evaluation speed (full-graph machine learning potentials) or geometric sensitivity (coordination-based models like the alpha-scheme).

posts.credit: Dwaipayan Dubey, Karan Molaverdikhani, Barbara Ercolano, et al. · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: A planet's air can reveal where and how it was born
posts.sub: Reading the chemistry of distant atmospheres helps astronomers retrace how planets form.
posts.author: Dwaipayan Dubey, Karan Molaverdikhani, Barbara Ercolano, et al.
posts.summary: Understanding the chemical diversity of exoplanet atmospheres is crucial for linking atmospheric composition to planetary formation history. Atmospheric C/O can provide clues about where and how planets form, particularly through the accretion of gas and solids across disk snowlines.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Chemistry as a birth certificate","p":["Planets form in discs of gas and dust around young stars, and different ingredients freeze into ice at different distances from the star. Those freezing boundaries are known as snowlines. A planet's atmosphere keeps a chemical record of the gas and solids it gathered along the way."]},{"h":"What the work shows","p":["The authors examine how the balance of carbon and oxygen in an exoplanet's atmosphere can act as a clue to its birthplace. Because that balance changes across the snowlines in the disc, measuring it helps trace where and how a planet assembled. The clue works because the disc's chemistry varies with distance."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Linking atmospheric chemistry to formation history is a step toward understanding how habitable worlds come to be. The carbon-to-oxygen balance acts like a chemical fingerprint of a planet's nursery. As telescopes read more atmospheres, this framework helps turn measurements into stories of planetary birth."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Reading exoplanet air to trace its birth
posts.orig_sub: Clues to how — and where — habitable worlds form.

posts.credit: Qunfeng Jiang · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: Lighter giant planets may spare their smaller neighbours
posts.sub: The finding changes how astronomers read the histories of distant planetary systems.
posts.author: Qunfeng Jiang
posts.summary: The survival of an inner planet next to a close-in giant is commonly used to argue against high-eccentricity migration (HEM), because the eccentric giant is expected to destabilize the inner system.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Giants on wild orbits","p":["Some giant planets end up orbiting very close to their stars. One leading explanation is a dramatic migration: the planet first swings on a long, stretched-out orbit that gradually shrinks and rounds off near the star. Such a sweeping giant was expected to wreck any smaller planets orbiting closer in."]},{"h":"What the study found","p":["The researcher shows that lower-mass giants can pass through this stretched-orbit migration without destroying their inner neighbours. Mass matters: lighter giants disturb their neighbours less. The survival of a small planet next to a close-in giant, long used as evidence against this migration route, turns out to be compatible with it."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["The result removes a common objection to one of the main theories of how giant planets move. It gives astronomers a more reliable way to reconstruct the violent histories of planetary systems beyond our own. It is a result about orbital dynamics."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Lower-Mass Giants Can Spare Inner Planets during High-Eccentricity Migration
posts.orig_sub: The survival of an inner planet next to a close-in giant is commonly used to argue against high-eccentricity migration (HEM), because the eccentric giant is expected to destabilize the inner system.

posts.credit: Michael A. Garrett · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: Study shows when a planet's radio signals can escape
posts.sub: Knowing which signals get out could help us detect magnetic fields on distant worlds.
posts.author: Michael A. Garrett
posts.summary: Radio emission generated on a planetary surface must cross the planet's ionosphere before escaping into space: below the local plasma frequency it is reflected back towards the surface.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"A planet's radio shield","p":["Planets can generate radio emission near their surfaces, and detecting it from afar is a promising way to find magnetic fields on distant worlds. Magnetic fields are thought to help protect a planet's atmosphere. But the signal must first pass through the ionosphere, an electrically charged layer of the upper atmosphere."]},{"h":"What the work explains","p":["The author works out when radio waves can escape and when they cannot. Below a characteristic frequency set by the charged particles in the ionosphere, the emission is reflected back toward the surface instead of leaking into space, so only signals above that cutoff reach our telescopes."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Magnetic fields help shape a planet's habitability, so a reliable way to detect them matters. The escape cutoff depends on the planet's own upper atmosphere. Knowing the conditions tells observers which frequencies to watch and how to interpret a silence. The work is theoretical."]}]}
posts.orig_title: When a planet's radio signals can escape
posts.orig_sub: A new way to detect magnetic fields on distant worlds.

posts.credit: Xianyu Tan, Yanhong Lai, Jinghao Zhang, et al. · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: Clouds reshuffle the weather on scorching giant planets
posts.sub: Better climate models of alien worlds help us read what telescopes see.
posts.author: Xianyu Tan, Yanhong Lai, Jinghao Zhang, et al.
posts.summary: We perform general circulation modeling of hot and ultra-hot Jupiters across equilibrium temperatures of T_eq=1600 to 2800 K, incorporating cloud formation and its feedback on atmospheric dynamics.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Weather on hot Jupiters","p":["Hot Jupiters are giant planets orbiting so close to their stars that their atmospheres reach temperatures of thousands of degrees. Astronomers simulate their global weather to understand observations, but clouds have often been left out of the picture. Astronomers cannot visit these worlds, so models do the work."]},{"h":"What the team modelled","p":["The researchers ran climate simulations of hot and ultra-hot Jupiters across a wide range of temperatures, this time including cloud formation and its feedback on the atmospheric flow. The clouds are not just decoration: they change how heat is absorbed and moved, reshaping the circulation."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Including clouds makes the simulated climates of these worlds more realistic, which helps astronomers interpret telescope measurements of their atmospheres. It is a modelling advance that sharpens our picture of weather far beyond the solar system. The result is a more complete picture of their weather."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Clouds reshape the weather of hot Jupiters
posts.orig_sub: Better models of climates on alien worlds.

posts.credit: Takashi Shimokawa, Masahiro Machida, Yoshihiro Kawasaki · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: Simulations link magnetic fields to planet-building dust
posts.sub: The work probes how magnetic stirring in young discs affects the first steps of planet formation.
posts.author: Takashi Shimokawa, Masahiro Machida, Yoshihiro Kawasaki
posts.summary: We performed one-dimensional calculations to investigate how the magnetorotational instability (MRI) affects dust growth in protoplanetary disks. We simultaneously solved the evolution of the dust size distribution and the vertical magnetic field.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"From dust to planets","p":["Planets begin as dust grains in the discs of gas around young stars, and those grains must somehow grow into larger bodies. Without that growth, there are no planets. Magnetic fields stir the gas in these discs, and that turbulence can help or hinder the dust's growth."]},{"h":"What the team calculated","p":["The researchers performed calculations that follow two things at once: how the sizes of dust grains evolve, and how the disc's vertical magnetic field changes over time. This let them study how magnetic stirring, driven by an instability in the swirling gas, depends on field strength and feeds back on dust growth."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["The earliest steps of planet building remain one of the field's open questions. Linking magnetic field strength to dust growth gives modellers a more complete picture of how planetary systems, including our own, get started. The study is theoretical, modelling one slice of the disc."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Dependence of Dust Growth on Magnetic field Strength in Protoplanetary Disks
posts.orig_sub: We performed one-dimensional calculations to investigate how the magnetorotational instability (MRI) affects dust growth in protoplanetary disks. We simultaneously solved the evolution of the dust size distribution and the vertical magnetic field.

posts.credit: Lisa Kaltenegger, Abigail Bohl, Connor Novak, et al. · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: Researchers explore why Venus and Earth grew so different
posts.sub: The tale of two similar planets holds lessons for what keeps a world habitable.
posts.author: Lisa Kaltenegger, Abigail Bohl, Connor Novak, et al.
posts.summary: Venus and Earth, planets with similar masses and radii, provide astonishingly different environments, raising the question of why these two rocky worlds evolved so differently. Explaining this divergence is a central challenge in comparative planetology and astrobiology.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Twins with opposite fates","p":["Venus and Earth are near-twins in size and mass, yet their environments could hardly be more different. Why two similar rocky worlds evolved along such opposite paths is a central challenge in comparing planets and assessing habitability. The contrast is one of planetary science's most striking open puzzles."]},{"h":"What the work examines","p":["The authors examine the divergence of the two planets, treating them as a natural experiment in how rocky worlds develop. Comparing their histories helps isolate the factors that pushed one toward a livable climate and the other toward extremes. The question sits at the heart of comparative planetology and astrobiology."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Understanding what kept Earth habitable, and what made Venus hostile, guides the search for livable planets around other stars. It also informs how we judge distant Earth-like worlds, and frames the question of how stable our own planet's climate really is."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Why Venus and Earth took opposite paths
posts.orig_sub: Lessons for what keeps a planet habitable.

posts.credit: Anastasia Triantafillides, Jason S. Pero, Angelique Kahle, et al. · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: Astronomers work to see through the haze of sub-Neptunes
posts.sub: These hazy worlds are the galaxy's most common known planet type, yet remain hard to read.
posts.author: Anastasia Triantafillides, Jason S. Pero, Angelique Kahle, et al.
posts.summary: Among the current population of exoplanets there are very few sub-Neptunes that have their atmospheric composition identified. This is primarily due to sub-Neptunes having high metallicity, clouds, and/or hazes obscuring absorption features.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The most common mystery","p":["Sub-Neptunes, planets smaller than Neptune but larger than Earth, are among the most common worlds known in the galaxy. Yet for very few of them do astronomers know what their atmospheres are actually made of. Reading their air is the next frontier."]},{"h":"Why they are hard to read","p":["The trouble is that these atmospheres tend to be rich in heavier elements and wrapped in clouds or hazes. Those layers flatten or hide the chemical fingerprints that telescopes look for. The result is a blurred signal with few identifiable features, leaving the composition ambiguous even for well-studied planets."]},{"h":"What comes next","p":["The work addresses how to peer through these obscuring layers and identify what sub-Neptune atmospheres contain. Better reading of these atmospheres would test theories of how such planets form. Cracking the most common planet type would fill a major gap in our picture of worlds beyond the solar system."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Peering through the haze of sub-Neptunes
posts.orig_sub: Unmasking the most common kind of planet in the galaxy.

posts.credit: Elina Y. Zhang, Fei Dai, Yaguang Li, et al. · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: Astronomers revisit the spin puzzle of a dying planet
posts.sub: The case tests our picture of how stars slowly swallow their closest planets.
posts.author: Elina Y. Zhang, Fei Dai, Yaguang Li, et al.
posts.summary: WASP-12 b is the only exoplanet with confirmed orbital decay. Angular momentum transferred from its decaying orbit should have realigned the star's thin convective layer, yet an earlier Rossiter--McLaughlin (RM) measurement suggested a \sim60^\circ spin--orbit misalignment.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"A planet falling inward","p":["WASP-12 b is a planet spiralling toward its star, the only exoplanet with confirmed orbital decay. As its orbit shrinks, the planet should transfer its motion to the star's thin outer layer, gradually lining up the star's spin with the orbit. It is a unique case among known exoplanets."]},{"h":"The puzzle","p":["An earlier measurement suggested the star's spin was tilted by about sixty degrees from the orbit, which did not fit that tidy picture. The new study re-examines this apparent misalignment, testing what the star's orientation really says about the planet's doomed journey. That mismatch was the puzzle the team set out to resolve."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["This system is the best natural laboratory for watching a star consume a planet, offering a rare chance to see orbital decay in action. Getting its geometry right sharpens the theories astronomers use to predict the fates of close-in planets elsewhere."]}]}
posts.orig_title: A dying planet's spin puzzle resolved
posts.orig_sub: Testing how stars swallow their closest planets.

posts.credit: William O. Balmer, William Thompson, Rodrigo P. Silva, et al. · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: A planet's orbit shape records its turbulent history
posts.sub: Reading how stretched an orbit is helps astronomers retrace a planet's past and future.
posts.author: William O. Balmer, William Thompson, Rodrigo P. Silva, et al.
posts.summary: The eccentricity of an exoplanet's orbit is a key observational quantity that can be used to infer its dynamical past and predict its future orbital evolution. Planets are expected to emerge from their protoplanetary cradles with roughly circular eccentricities, and non-circular eccentricites to arise from subsequent
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Circles and ellipses","p":["Planets are expected to emerge from their birth discs on nearly circular orbits. The stretch of an orbit is called its eccentricity. When astronomers instead find a stretched, elliptical path, something must have disturbed the planet later, perhaps a gravitational encounter with another world. The birth disc sets the initial, nearly circular path."]},{"h":"What the work explores","p":["The authors examine how eccentricity can be used as a record of a planet's dynamical past. A nearly circular orbit suggests a calm history. Because the same quantity also governs how the orbit will keep evolving, measuring it lets researchers both reconstruct history and forecast what comes next."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Orbit shapes are one of the few clues available about events that happened long ago in distant systems. Using them well turns a simple measurement into a story of migrations and close encounters, history and forecast written into a single number."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Orbit shapes reveal a planet's past
posts.orig_sub: Predicting the future of distant worlds.

posts.credit: Biel Escolà-Rodrigo · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: A faster way to sort real planets from false alarms
posts.sub: Speeding up the checks clears the backlog of promising worlds waiting to be studied.
posts.author: Biel Escolà-Rodrigo
posts.summary: The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) continues to identify thousands of transit candidates that require statistical validation to rule out astrophysical false positives before atmospheric characterization can be pursued.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Too many candidates","p":["A space telescope that watches stars for the telltale dips of passing planets keeps finding thousands of candidate worlds. Many turn out to be false alarms, such as pairs of stars mimicking a planet's signal, so each candidate needs checking before serious study. Each dip in a star's light could be a planet."]},{"h":"What the work offers","p":["The author presents a faster approach to statistically validating these candidates, the calculations that estimate how likely a signal is to be a genuine planet rather than an astrophysical impostor. Speeding up this vetting helps separate real worlds from lookalikes more efficiently."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Only confirmed planets move on to the expensive next step, studying their atmospheres. A quicker vetting pipeline clears the path for telescopes to focus on the most promising new worlds instead of waiting in line. The method targets the thousands of candidates the survey keeps producing."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Faster vetting of TESS planet candidates
posts.orig_sub: Clearing the path to study promising new worlds.

posts.credit: Emma V. Turtelboom, William Thompson, Ryan Cloutier, et al. · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: Astronomers find a heavy outer world in a rhythmic planetary system
posts.sub: A distant giant orbiting far beyond six small planets could help explain how their rare orbital rhythm survives.
posts.author: Emma V. Turtelboom, William Thompson, Ryan Cloutier, et al.
posts.summary: We report the discovery of a massive outer companion around TOI-178, a known planetary system with six inner small planets within 0.15 AU, five of which are in a 2:4:6:9:12 resonant chain.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"What they found","p":["Astronomers report a massive companion orbiting far outside the known planets of TOI-178, a star already famous for hosting six small worlds packed tightly together. The newly found object lies well beyond that close-knit inner family, making the system considerably larger than previously thought."]},{"h":"A system in rhythm","p":["Five of the six inner planets move in a linked pattern, their orbital periods keeping time with one another like a celestial metronome. Such orderly arrangements are rare and easily disturbed by passing worlds, so they preserve valuable clues about how the whole system formed and evolved."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Adding a heavy outer member changes the picture of this system's history. Working out how the distant companion and the inner chain fit together could help astronomers understand how such delicate orbital rhythms survive over billions of years, and what else might be hiding in similar systems."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Discovery of a Massive Outer Companion to the TOI-178 Resonant Chain
posts.orig_sub: We report the discovery of a massive outer companion around TOI-178, a known planetary system with six inner small planets within 0.15 AU, five of which are in a 2:4:6:9:12 resonant chain.

posts.credit: Ailar Alizadehsabegh, Soroush Sarabi, Atila Poro · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: A fair test bed for guessing what distant planets are made of
posts.sub: A shared benchmark lets scientists compare methods that estimate what planets around other stars are made of.
posts.author: Ailar Alizadehsabegh, Soroush Sarabi, Atila Poro
posts.summary: The mass-radius (M-R) relation is fundamental to inferring the bulk composition and internal structure of exoplanets. However, published relations remain difficult to compare directly because studies adopt different planetary samples, fitting procedures, and evaluation metrics.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The problem","p":["To guess what a distant planet is made of, astronomers combine its mass and size. But published recipes for linking the two are hard to compare, because each study uses different planet samples, different fitting methods and different scoring rules, leaving the field without a common yardstick."]},{"h":"What the team did","p":["The researchers built a single, uniform benchmark for these mass-size relationships. By putting every method on the same footing, the work makes it possible to judge which approaches genuinely describe planets best, rather than which happened to be tested under the most favourable conditions."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Better comparisons mean more trustworthy estimates of whether a world is rocky, watery or gassy. That sharpened picture feeds directly into studies of how planets form, and helps astronomers decide which distant worlds are worth a closer look with powerful telescopes."]}]}
posts.orig_title: A Homogeneous Benchmark of Exoplanet Mass-Radius Relations
posts.orig_sub: The mass-radius (M-R) relation is fundamental to inferring the bulk composition and internal structure of exoplanets. However, published relations remain difficult to compare directly because studies adopt different planetary samples, fitting procedures, and evaluation metrics.

posts.credit: M. Rumenskikh, S. S. Sharipov, I. F. Shaikhislamov, et al. · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: A new way to spot magnetic shields around distant planets
posts.sub: Magnetic fields can shield a planet's atmosphere, so finding them helps judge which distant worlds could support life.
posts.author: M. Rumenskikh, S. S. Sharipov, I. F. Shaikhislamov, et al.
posts.summary: A method for detecting the intrinsic magnetic fields of exoplanets, based on the effect of atomic alignment (the redistribution of populations among magnetic sublevels under the action of anisotropic radiation from the host star), has been adapted for observations with the Spektr-UV space telescope.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Why magnetic fields matter","p":["A planet's magnetic field acts like an invisible shield, deflecting harmful particles streaming from its star. On Earth it helps keep our atmosphere and surface habitable, so spotting similar shields around other stars' planets is a key step in the search for life beyond our solar system."]},{"h":"What the team did","p":["The researchers adapted a method that reads subtle changes in starlight passing through a planet's surroundings. These changes, caused by atoms lining up under the star's light, reveal the planet's own magnetic field. They tailored the technique for observations with the Spektr-UV space telescope."]},{"h":"What comes next","p":["If the approach works in practice, astronomers could survey magnetic shields on worlds far beyond our solar system. That would add a practical new clue when deciding which planets deserve deeper study as possible homes for life, complementing other signs of habitability."]}]}
posts.orig_title: A new probe of exoplanet magnetic fields
posts.orig_sub: Spotting shields that could protect alien life.

posts.credit: Bingjie Zha, Zhuo Chen · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: Sharper models reveal how giant planets get their first heat
posts.sub: Understanding a young giant planet's starting temperature helps explain how worlds like Jupiter grow and cool.
posts.author: Bingjie Zha, Zhuo Chen
posts.summary: Within the core-accretion framework, gas giants acquire most of their mass through accretion shocks during runaway gas accretion. The shock thermodynamics---governed by radiative cooling, accretion history, and equation of state (EoS)---sets the post-shock gas entropy and initial thermal state, strongly influencing
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The birth of giants","p":["Giant planets like Jupiter are thought to grow by pulling in huge amounts of gas once a solid core is in place. As that gas crashes onto the growing planet, it passes through a violent boundary that heats it up, setting the newborn world's initial temperature."]},{"h":"What the team studied","p":["The researchers examined how that crashing gas sets a newborn planet's starting heat. Their models track how cooling, the planet's growth history and the behaviour of hot gas together decide how much warmth the young world keeps, refining the picture of how gas giants are born."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["A planet's first heat shapes how it shrinks and cools for billions of years afterwards. Sharper models of this starting point could help astronomers read the histories of real giant planets from the light we see today, and better understand how worlds like Jupiter came to be."]}]}
posts.orig_title: How gas giants get their first heat
posts.orig_sub: Sharper models of how planets are born.

posts.credit: Michaela Walterová, Marie Běhounková · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: Tides between neighbouring worlds matter more than we thought
posts.sub: In tightly packed planetary systems, moons and planets can tug on each other, reshaping orbits and internal heating.
posts.author: Michaela Walterová, Marie Běhounková
posts.summary: Almost negligible among the solar system planets, mutual tides raised by a secondary on another secondary orbiting the same primary may gain increased importance in tightly packed systems, e.g., between the components of close-in exoplanetary systems or between the moons of gas giants.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"A familiar force, new setting","p":["Tides are the gentle stretching pulls that worlds exert on one another. In our solar system, the tides that moons raise on neighbouring moons are almost negligible, so modellers have usually been able to ignore them when tracking how orbits change over long stretches of time."]},{"h":"What the team found","p":["The researchers show that in tightly packed systems, such as close-in families of exoplanets or the moons of giant planets, these mutual tides can grow important. Neighbouring worlds pull on each other strongly enough to matter for the system's long-term evolution, contrary to the usual assumption."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Tidal stretching can heat a world's interior and shift its orbit, both of which affect habitability. Including these neighbour-to-neighbour tides could give more realistic pictures of how crowded planetary systems, and their potentially habitable moons, change over billions of years."]}]}
posts.orig_title: Tides between moons and close planets matter
posts.orig_sub: Refining the dynamics of tightly packed systems.

posts.credit: Kevin Ollmann, Romain Laugier, Jeremy P. Scott, et al. · arXiv · astro-ph.EP
posts.title: A telescope technique takes aim at hot dust around nearby stars
posts.sub: Blazing dust close to other stars can hide Earth-like planets, so a new observing approach aims to study it.
posts.author: Kevin Ollmann, Romain Laugier, Jeremy P. Scott, et al.
posts.summary: Near-infrared interferometric surveys have revealed extended emission around the photosphere of \approx 40 main-sequence stars, attributed to the presence of hot exozodiacal dust (HEZD). A promising technique for investigating this phenomenon is nulling interferometry.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The dusty puzzle","p":["Surveys have found glowing clouds of hot dust hugging roughly forty Sun-like stars. This dust, thought to be the crushed remains of comets or asteroids, shines brightly enough to interfere with attempts to image small, faint planets that may be orbiting nearby."]},{"h":"What the team did","p":["The researchers assessed a technique called nulling interferometry, which combines light from several telescopes so that a star's glare cancels out while the surrounding dust remains visible. They examined its prospects for studying this hot dust in detail using the Very Large Telescope Interferometer."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Understanding the dust is a stepping stone to seeing Earth-like worlds. If the technique delivers, astronomers could map these dusty regions and clear a major obstacle on the road to photographing potentially habitable planets around other stars."]}]}

posts.orig_sub: Near-infrared interferometric surveys have revealed extended emission around the photosphere of \approx 40 main-sequence stars, attributed to the presence of hot exozodiacal dust (HEZD). A promising technique for investigating this phenomenon is nulling interferometry.

posts.credit: Eliot J. Kim, Eric J. Mei, Peter D. Ivatt, et al. · arXiv · physics.ao-ph
posts.title: Scientists work to track the atmosphere's methane cleanup crew

posts.credit: Samet Demir, Zafer Dogan · arXiv · stat.ML
posts.title: Study unpacks the quirks of how neural networks train
posts.sub: Researchers trace how noisy training steps shape what a simple neural network ultimately learns.
posts.author: Samet Demir, Zafer Dogan
posts.summary: We study two-layer neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a multi-index teacher model, focusing on how first-layer parameters orthogonal to the teacher subspace affect generalization.

The noise makes training erratic, and understanding its effects on what the model learns is an active research question. Those noisy updates are not just a nuisance; they may shape which solutions the network finds and how well it generalises."]},{"h":"What they did","p":["The team analysed simple two-layer networks learning from a controlled, artificial teacher model. They separated the training dynamics into distinct effects, including sudden spikes linked to the teacher and a build-up of randomness in parts of the network unrelated to the task."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Pinning down these effects helps explain why networks sometimes generalise well and sometimes poorly. posts.title: A unified recipe for building AI models that respect symmetry
posts.sub: Mathematicians unify scattered techniques for building models that treat rotated or shifted inputs consistently.

posts.summary: We present a general framework for modeling and learning equivariant functions between finite dimensional semisimple real group representations, unifying constructions developed across many application areas.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The idea","p":["Many problems have built-in symmetry: rotating a molecule or shifting an image should not change the underlying answer. Models that respect these symmetries, called equivariant models, often learn better and need less data than models that ignore them.","Building that respect into the model's structure, rather than hoping it learns the symmetry from examples alone, is the guiding principle of this line of work."]},{"h":"What they did","p":["The researchers present a general mathematical framework for building such models using polynomial features, unifying constructions that had been developed separately across many application areas. It offers one common recipe instead of many separate tricks."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["A shared foundation makes it easier to design symmetry-aware models for chemistry, physics and imaging, and to understand how the existing approaches relate. The rules deciding whose positions get cut, and in what order, raise questions of fairness and risk. If users can game the rule by reshuffling their accounts, the system's fairness and its financial safety both suffer at once."]},{"h":"What they did","p":["The researchers characterised all rules whose outcome depends only on the final state, not the path taken. posts.title: New review urges better checks on big investment models
posts.sub: Models that guide huge climate and energy investments are only useful if their assumptions are properly tested.

posts.summary: Real options (RO) modeling provides a powerful framework for valuing managerial flexibility under uncertainty in capital-intensive investments across various industries, including climate, energy, and transportation. posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Valuing the freedom to wait","p":["When companies plan costly projects in climate, energy or transport, the future is uncertain. A modelling approach called real options puts a value on staying flexible, such as waiting or changing course later, instead of committing everything up front. These decisions can involve enormous sums and span decades, so the quality of the underlying modelling really counts."]},{"h":"What the review examined","p":["The authors systematically reviewed how these studies test their assumptions, a step known as sensitivity analysis. This means checking how much the answer changes when key inputs change. They found that the transparency and usefulness of these models depend heavily on doing this well. posts.credit: Sai Niranjan Ramachandran · arXiv · cs.LG
posts.title: Study links automated trading to markets' jagged price swings
posts.sub: Computer-driven trading may help explain why market prices jitter in an unusually rough, erratic way.
posts.author: Sai Niranjan Ramachandran
posts.summary: Existing work suggests that markets can show volatility with paths rougher than those of Brownian motion. In theory this can happen when the order flow is close to instability with memory that decays as a power law.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"A puzzle in market data","p":["Market prices are always jittery, but studies suggest their swings can be rougher and more erratic than the standard mathematical picture of random motion predicts. Explaining where that extra roughness comes from has been an open question in market research. The standard picture treats price moves like the smooth wanderings of a drifting particle, an idea borrowed from physics."]},{"h":"What the study argues","p":["This work connects that roughness to automated market making, the software that continuously offers to buy and sell. In theory, when the flow of orders sits close to instability and its after-effects fade only slowly, the resulting price paths turn unusually jagged."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["If automated trading itself shapes how wild prices look, that changes how researchers and risk managers think about market stability. It suggests some of the market's roughness is built into how modern trading works, rather than coming purely from outside news."]}]}

posts.credit: Paul Glasserman, Mike Li, Dan Pirjol · arXiv · q-fin.MF
posts.title: Researchers uncover a tidy pattern in American option prices
posts.sub: Option prices turn out to follow an orderly rule as their expiry dates stretch further away.
posts.author: Paul Glasserman, Mike Li, Dan Pirjol
posts.summary: Call option prices, viewed as functions of strike and time-to-expiration, are totally positive of order 2 (TP2) if the ratio of the price of a higher-strike call to a lower-strike call increases with time-to-expiration. A corresponding property applies to put option prices.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"What options are","p":["An option is a contract giving the right to buy or sell an asset at an agreed price before a deadline. American-style options can be used at any time up to that deadline, making their pricing harder to pin down. Because they can be exercised early, working out what they are worth involves choices as well as probabilities."]},{"h":"What the team found","p":["The authors show these prices obey a strict ordering rule. Comparing two contracts with different agreed prices, the ratio between their values rises steadily as the time left to expiry grows. A matching rule holds for contracts giving the right to sell."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Hidden regularities like this give researchers firm ground rules that any pricing model must respect. That can help check models for errors and deepen the mathematical understanding of contracts traded on markets every day. It is basic research with practical downstream value."]}]}

posts.title: Leaner training method helps scientific models learn as they run
posts.sub: Simulations that blend physics with AI could keep improving themselves while using far less computing power.

posts.credit: Wei Zou, Jizhou Li, Xurui He, et al. · arXiv · physics.ao-ph
posts.title: Hidden wind boundaries may explain storms' split path forecasts
posts.sub: A new idea could help forecasters know when a cyclone's predicted track is about to fork.
posts.author: Wei Zou, Jizhou Li, Xurui He, et al.
posts.summary: Tropical cyclones whose predicted tracks bifurcate are among the most dreaded storms in disaster planning. Understanding when and why these bifurcations occur has been a long-standing puzzle in track forecasting. We address this issue by introducing the concept of "fate boundaries" hidden in the steering flow.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The forecasters' nightmare","p":["Some tropical cyclones sit at a crossroads: small differences in the forecast send them down completely different paths, towards different coasts. These splitting predictions are among the most dreaded situations in disaster planning, and knowing when and why they happen has been a long-standing puzzle. Evacuation decisions can hinge on which branch of the forecast a storm ultimately takes."]},{"h":"What the team proposes","p":["The researchers introduce the idea of fate boundaries hidden inside the winds that steer a storm. Think of an invisible dividing line in the atmosphere: a cyclone on one side is carried one way, while one just across it ends up somewhere else entirely."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["If forecasters can spot these boundaries, they could better judge when track predictions are genuinely fragile and communicate that uncertainty earlier. That could give coastal communities more useful warning before a storm commits to its path. It is early-stage work, but it targets a genuinely dangerous blind spot."]}]}

posts.title: Study explains why hurricanes rarely form near the equator
posts.sub: Warm ocean fuel is everywhere in the tropics, but storms also need a spin ingredient the equator lacks.
posts.author: Boris Galperin, Jun A. Zhang
posts.summary: Tropical cyclones almost never form within a few degrees of the equator. Their energy source, the heat engine fueled by the warm ocean, is available there as everywhere else. posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"A gap on the map","p":["Tropical cyclones almost never form within a few degrees of the equator, even though the warm ocean water that powers them is just as available there as anywhere else in the tropics. Near the equator this background spin is too weak for a storm to organise. The paper weighs the roles of spin and raw energy in getting a cyclone started."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Knowing which ingredient controls where storms can be born sharpens the basic picture of hurricane formation. That understanding underpins the models forecasters rely on, and helps explain why the equator itself stays remarkably storm-free despite its warm seas. It is a reminder that a storm needs the right conditions, not just warm water."]}]}

posts.credit: Sara Shamekh, Viviana Acquaviva · arXiv · physics.ao-ph
posts.title: Study links measurement design to pinning down chaotic models
posts.sub: Getting useful answers from chaotic models depends on how long and how often you observe them.
posts.author: Sara Shamekh, Viviana Acquaviva
posts.summary: Parameter estimation in chaotic models often relies on prescribed summary statistics, whose ability to constrain parameters may be difficult to establish in advance. Different parameters influence different features and time scales of the dynamics, so the record length and sampling interval needed to constrain them
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The chaos problem","p":["Chaotic systems, from turbulent fluids to parts of the climate, are famously twitchy: tiny changes grow into big ones. Estimating the settings of a model that describes them usually relies on chosen summary statistics, and it can be hard to know in advance whether those summaries actually pin the settings down."]},{"h":"What the team worked out","p":["The researchers connect the question to time itself. Different model settings leave their fingerprints on different features and different time scales of the behaviour. So the length of the observational record, and how frequently it is sampled, determine which settings can be reliably estimated at all."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["This gives scientists a principled way to design measurement campaigns before collecting data, rather than discovering afterwards that the observations could never answer the question. It is a methods advance for anyone modelling unpredictable natural systems. The work helps turn observation planning from guesswork into a reasoned design choice."]}]}

posts.title: Evidence review concludes the Atlantic's great current is slowing
posts.sub: A vast ocean circulation that shapes climate appears to be weakening, as models long predicted.
posts.author: Stefan Rahmstorf, Levke Caesar
posts.summary: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a critical component of the climate system. Climate models have long predicted a slowing of the AMOC due to anthropogenic forcing, with a risk of passing tipping points in the future.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The ocean's conveyor belt","p":["The Atlantic hosts a vast circulation that carries warm water north and cold water back south, helping shape the climate of the surrounding continents. Scientists call it the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, and it is considered a critical component of the climate system. Its strength influences weather far beyond the ocean itself, from Europe to the tropics."]},{"h":"What the authors conclude","p":["Climate models have long predicted that human-driven warming would slow this circulation, with a risk of crossing dangerous tipping points in the future. Weighing the available evidence, the authors of this paper conclude that the balance of it indicates the slowdown is already under way."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["A weaker circulation could shift rainfall, temperatures and sea levels around the Atlantic. Confirming the trend, and understanding its pace, matters for everyone planning coastal defences, farming and infrastructure over the coming decades. The stakes are long-term and continental in scale."]}]}

posts.credit: Richard J. Murchie, Petronilo Martin-Iglesias, Julian Hofmann, et al. · arXiv · quant-ph
posts.title: Atom-based sensor tested as a new way to detect terahertz waves
posts.sub: A gap between electronics and light technology makes this kind of sensing hard, and atoms may help.
posts.author: Richard J. Murchie, Petronilo Martin-Iglesias, Julian Hofmann, et al.
posts.summary: THz receiver technology lies between electronics and photonics; as such, its implementation is not as mature. This warrants investigation into alternative THz receivers such as Rydberg atom sensors, which are highly susceptible to electric fields.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"An awkward slice of the spectrum","p":["Terahertz radiation sits between radio waves and visible light, and the technology for detecting it is comparatively immature: it falls in a gap where neither conventional electronics nor light-based photonics works comfortably. That makes better receivers a standing engineering challenge."]},{"h":"What the team analysed","p":["The researchers assessed a receiver concept built on Rydberg atoms, atoms excited into states that make them extremely sensitive to electric fields. Because terahertz waves are electric fields oscillating very fast, such atoms are a natural candidate sensor. The paper analyses how well the concept could perform. No working instrument is claimed yet; the paper weighs the concept's expected performance."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Terahertz sensing is valuable for observing Earth and its atmosphere. This is an early-stage concept study, but if atom-based receivers prove practical, they could open a new route to instruments that today's technology struggles to build. posts.credit: Matteo Broccoli, Andrea Cipollone, Antonio Bonaduce, et al. · arXiv · physics.ao-ph
posts.title: AI improves spotting of ocean swirls in satellite sea-level data
posts.sub: Giant rotating currents move heat and life around the ocean, and finding them reliably matters.
posts.author: Matteo Broccoli, Andrea Cipollone, Antonio Bonaduce, et al.
posts.summary: Physically-based eddy detection algorithms usually rely on hard-coded thresholds and constraints that make the detected structures sensitive to small variations in the underlying fields.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Swirls that shape the sea","p":["The ocean is full of eddies, vast rotating swirls of water that carry heat, nutrients and marine life across great distances. These swirls can span vast distances and persist for months as they drift across ocean basins.","Satellites can spot them from the subtle bumps and dips they leave on the sea surface, and new wide-swath instruments map those bumps in unprecedented detail."]},{"h":"What the team changed","p":["Traditional detection algorithms rely on hard-coded thresholds, so their results can flip when the underlying data shifts slightly. The researchers instead trained data-driven models that combine several kinds of information at once, aiming for eddy detection that is steadier and less sensitive to small variations in the measurements."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Reliable eddy maps feed into ocean forecasting, climate studies and fisheries. If learned models prove more robust than rule-based ones, the censuses of these swirls that scientists rely on could become noticeably more trustworthy."]}]}

posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Land got there first","p":["Foundation models, large AI systems trained broadly so they can tackle many tasks, have recently transformed how scientists analyse Earth observation. The ocean has been left comparatively underserved by these general-purpose tools."]},{"h":"What the team built","p":["The researchers present DARWIN, a foundation model designed for marine data. posts.credit: Tao Li, Zhu Deng, Philippe Ciais, et al. · arXiv · physics.ao-ph
posts.title: Researchers project daily global carbon emissions for 2026
posts.sub: Waiting years for official emissions tallies leaves the world guessing about its own progress.

posts.summary: Global fossil-fuel combustion and industrial-process CO2 emissions remain close to historical highs, yet the recent slowdown in growth is difficult to assess before conventional inventories become available. We project emissions for 2026 and examine daily departures during major climate and energy disruptions.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Flying partly blind","p":["Global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels and industry remain close to historical highs. Growth has recently slowed, but judging that slowdown is difficult, because conventional emissions inventories arrive only after a long delay.","By the time the official numbers land, the world has moved on. Policymakers negotiating climate targets need to know whether the curve is bending now, not years ago."]},{"h":"What the team did","p":["The researchers project global emissions for 2026 at daily resolution, rather than waiting for the annual totals. They also examine day-by-day departures from the expected path during major climate and energy disruptions, showing how events knock emissions off course in close to real time."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Timely emissions estimates let governments and researchers see whether climate efforts are working while there is still time to adjust. A daily picture turns a once-a-year verdict into something closer to a running dashboard."]}]}

Ships and buoys cannot be everywhere, so most of the sea surface is never directly measured."]},{"h":"What the team built","p":["The researchers trained a machine learning system that fills the gaps between observations. posts.credit: Anastassia M. Makarieva, Andrei V. Nefiodov · arXiv · physics.ao-ph
posts.title: Water's cycle may be a major engine of the winds
posts.sub: Scientists are measuring how much of the atmosphere's power comes from evaporating and condensing water.
posts.author: Anastassia M. Makarieva, Andrei V. Nefiodov
posts.summary: Earth's atmosphere operates a steam cycle: water evaporates from the surface, expands as vapor, condenses in colder air, and returns as precipitation. Yet its power and relationship to atmospheric mechanical power remain poorly quantified.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The atmosphere's steam cycle","p":["Earth's air works a bit like a steam engine. Water evaporates from the surface, spreads out as vapour, condenses in colder air and falls back as rain or snow. This cycle is always running. Yet its strength has been hard to pin down."]},{"h":"What the researchers examined","p":["The team studied the push that water vapour gives the air as it expands and condenses. Surprisingly, the power of this process, and how it compares with the total energy of atmospheric motion, has never been well measured. They argue it deserves a central place in the picture."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Their work suggests this water-driven push is a major source of the energy behind winds and weather. Understanding it better could improve how scientists describe the atmosphere's power budget. It is a fresh look at an old, familiar cycle that shapes daily weather. The findings still need wider checking."]}]}

posts.credit: Shuochen Wang, Mark S. Allen, Auroop R. Ganguly · arXiv · physics.ao-ph
posts.title: New method trims outliers to sharpen hurricane track forecasts
posts.sub: Evacuation decisions depend on where a storm is heading, and stray forecast runs can blur the picture.
posts.author: Shuochen Wang, Mark S. Allen, Auroop R. Ganguly
posts.summary: Accurate tropical cyclone (TC) track guidance is essential for warnings, evacuation planning, and risk communication, but outlying members and distinct track scenarios can degrade raw ensemble forecasts.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Many forecasts, one storm","p":["Forecasters predict tropical cyclone paths by running many simulations at once, an ensemble, and looking at where they agree. Accurate track guidance is essential for warnings, evacuation planning and risk communication, so anything that muddies the ensemble's message carries real consequences.","A single simulation can miss; the crowd of simulations is usually wiser, but only if its outliers are handled well. Conflicting scenarios leave officials weighing very different futures for the same storm."]},{"h":"What the team improved","p":["Outlying runs and sharply different track scenarios can degrade the raw ensemble forecast. The researchers developed an objective method to reduce these track errors, tightening the spread of predictions so the guidance reflects the most credible paths rather than being dragged around by strays."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Sharper track forecasts mean better decisions about who evacuates and when. Even modest improvements in guidance can translate into safer, less disruptive responses as a storm approaches land."]}]}

posts.credit: Juyeon Kim, Chaeyeon Yi, Yun Am Seo · arXiv · stat.AP
posts.title: Frost warning AI gains a physics module, no leaf sensors needed
posts.sub: Farmers need local frost alerts to protect crops, even where no sensors sit on the plants themselves.
posts.author: Juyeon Kim, Chaeyeon Yi, Yun Am Seo
posts.summary: Frost protection requires local warnings where leaf-sensor inputs are unavailable. In the frost literature we surveyed, physics entered machine-learning models through inputs, numerical-model coupling, or losses, rather than model structure.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Protecting crops from frost","p":["A surprise overnight frost can damage an entire harvest, so growers need timely, short-term local warnings. The most direct systems read sensors attached to leaves, but most fields have none. Forecasting frost for those places means relying on weather data and models instead. Sprinklers, covers and heaters can save a crop, but only if switched on in time."]},{"h":"What the team built","p":["The researchers surveyed existing frost forecasting work and found that physics usually entered AI models through their inputs or training, not their structure. They instead designed a plug-in module, built on the energy balance of freezing, that slots into a modern forecasting model without needing leaf sensors."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Baking the physics of freezing into the model itself could make warnings more trustworthy where measurements are thin. For growers, that may mean earlier, more reliable notice to shield vulnerable crops on cold nights."]}]}

posts.credit: Kaushal Gianchandani, Luka Todorovic, Sai Ravela · arXiv · physics.comp-ph
posts.title: Neural networks run fluid simulations without any training
posts.sub: A network built straight from physics equations can simulate flowing water and air without learning from data.
posts.author: Kaushal Gianchandani, Luka Todorovic, Sai Ravela
posts.summary: Equation-derived neural integration can execute prescribed dynamics without training, while informative ensemble learning can estimate uncertain parameters and identify governing interactions without requiring differentiability.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Physics without the training","p":["Most scientific AI learns from data. This work takes a different route: the researchers build a neural network directly from the equations describing rotating shallow-water flow, a standard simplified picture of how oceans and atmospheres move on a spinning planet. The network runs those dynamics without any training."]},{"h":"Filling in the unknowns","p":["Real systems have uncertain settings and interactions. Alongside the equation-built network, the team uses ensemble learning, running many candidate versions together, to estimate uncertain parameters and identify which interactions govern the behaviour, without requiring the special mathematical properties some methods demand."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["The combination offers a way to simulate geophysical flows that respects known physics while still learning what is unknown. It is early-stage methodology, but it hints at simulations that are both principled and adaptable. posts.credit: Onur Beker, A. René Geist, Michael Posa, et al. · arXiv · cs.RO
posts.title: New tutorial demystifies how robots simulate touching things
posts.sub: Realistic contact simulation underpins robot design and control, and a new guide makes it approachable.
posts.author: Onur Beker, A. René Geist, Michael Posa, et al.
posts.summary: Simulating rigid-body dynamics with contact is fundamental to robotics, from motion synthesis and control to mechanism design. Many widely used simulators rely on cone complementarity formulations, whose physical assumptions and numerical solution require substantial background.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"Why touch is hard","p":["For a robot, touching the world is the crucial moment: gripping, walking and assembling all hinge on contact. Simulating those moments faithfully is fundamental to robotics, underpinning how machines are designed, controlled and taught new movements before they ever touch real hardware. Get contact physics wrong in simulation, and a robot that worked on screen can fail in the lab."]},{"h":"What the tutorial offers","p":["Many popular simulators rely on a mathematical formulation of contact whose physical assumptions and numerical solution demand substantial background knowledge. This tutorial unpacks that formulation step by step, explaining what the mathematics assumes about the world and how the calculations actually work."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["When the tools behind robot simulation are understood by more people, they are used more correctly and improved more quickly. A clear entry point lowers the barrier for students and engineers building the next generation of machines."]}]}

posts.credit: Hao Vo, Taisei Hanyu, Yuki Ikebe, et al. · arXiv · cs.RO
posts.title: New benchmark tests whether robots understand everyday physics
posts.sub: Robot AI is mostly tested on gripping, so a new exam probes gravity, friction and how objects behave.
posts.author: Hao Vo, Taisei Hanyu, Yuki Ikebe, et al.

posts.title: A new way to forecast where moving people and vehicles will go
posts.sub: Better predictions of how traffic and crowds move could help machines plan safer paths around us.

posts.summary: Multimodal trajectory forecasting must cover diverse future behaviors without sacrificing dynamical coherence. Most generative forecasters evolve frame-wise positions directly, leaving the relationships among position, velocity, and acceleration implicit.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The challenge","p":["Machines that share space with people need to guess what happens next: where each person or vehicle might go, across several possible futures. A good forecast must cover that range of behaviors while staying physically sensible, with speed and acceleration that fit together naturally."]},{"h":"What the team changed","p":["Most forecasting systems predict positions frame by frame, leaving the links between position, speed and acceleration implicit. posts.title: Researchers rethink how robot control models pay attention

posts.summary: Prior work calls the high attention on the first and last action tokens of a flow-based VLA policy a radial action sink, and uses these tokens to set the execution horizon. In language models, a sink is a token with high incoming attention, a small value, and little effect on the output.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The accepted story","p":["Some robot control models turn language and vision into streams of actions. Earlier work noticed that these models pay heavy attention to the first and last items in that stream, called it an attention sink, and used those items to decide how long each burst of movement should run."]},{"h":"The re-examination","p":["In language models, a sink is a spot that draws attention but carries little information and barely affects the output. The new study asks whether the same label really fits robot action models, going beyond the sink interpretation to examine what this radial attention pattern actually does."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["If engineers misread where a robot's model is focusing, they may tune its behavior on false assumptions. posts.title: Robots get better at handling objects that refuse to sit still
posts.sub: Grabbing or moving something that is already in motion is hard for robots, and this model targets that gap.
posts.author: Yuxiang Yang, Jingbo Zhang, Jiaru Zhong, et al.
posts.summary: Predicting future scene or object states does not necessarily reveal how robot-object interactions will advance or hinder a task. This challenge is particularly pronounced in dynamic robotic manipulation, where objects continue moving during perception and execution.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"The moving-target problem","p":["Most robot manipulation assumes objects hold still while the machine looks and acts. In dynamic tasks the object keeps moving during both perception and execution, so a plan made a moment ago can already be wrong. Predicting where the scene will be next is not enough."]},{"h":"The team's insight","p":["Knowing future positions does not reveal whether the robot's interaction will push the task forward or set it back. PhysVAM, their physics-oriented model, focuses on the future value of actions: how robot-object interactions will advance or hinder the goal, rather than just forecasting the scene."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["The real world is full of moving things, from items on a conveyor to objects handed over by people. Robots that judge how their actions will play out against moving objects could handle far more useful jobs. This is early-stage modeling work, not yet a finished product."]}]}

posts.title: A two-stage approach sharpens how robots generate movements
posts.sub: Robot movement plans start rough and get refined, and treating those stages differently could improve precision.
posts.author: Zhengtu Liang, Qiwei Liang, Tao Lin, et al.
posts.summary: Flow-matching robot policies usually use one prediction target throughout action generation, even though recovering actions from noise and polishing nearly clean actions bring different challenges.
posts.blog: {"sections":[{"h":"One size does not fit","p":["Many robot control models generate actions by starting with noise and gradually shaping it into a clean movement. These flow-based policies usually predict the same kind of target throughout the whole process, even though the early and late stages pose quite different problems."]},{"h":"What the team did","p":["UniVEP splits the job in two. Recovering a rough action from noise and polishing an almost-clean action are different challenges, so the model unifies two prediction styles, velocity and endpoint, letting each stage use the target that suits it best instead of forcing one choice everywhere."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Smoother, more precise action generation could make robots steadier at everyday manipulation, from picking up cups to placing parts. The change is a refinement of how these models are trained, an early-stage improvement that other researchers can build on rather than a finished robot system."]}]}

posts.title: How cancer cells keep their DNA caps from wearing out
posts.sub: Understanding how tumours keep dividing endlessly points to ways treatments could shut that ability down.
posts.author: Nina Rembiałkowska, Mikołaj Sędzik, Monika Kisielewska, Wiktoria Łuniewska, Kamil Sebastianka, Klaudia Molik, Katarzyna Skinderowicz, Jacek Kuźnicki, Joanna Tunikowska, Julita Kulbacka
posts.summary: Telomeres are repetitive DNA sequences at the ends of chromosomes that protect against genomic instability and prevent unwanted DNA damage responses. In most somatic cells, telomeres progressively shorten with each division, limiting cellular lifespan. However, cancer cells bypass this limitation by activating telomerase or the alternative lengthening of telomeres, enabling unchecked proliferation and tumor progression. This review examines the molecular mechanisms underlying telomere maintenance and their intricate relationship with DNA repair pathways. We discuss how telomere-associated proteins regulate genomic stability and explore therapeutic strategies targeting telomerase and alternative lengthening of telomeres. Challenges such as resistance mechanisms and off-target effects are also considered, highlighting the need for precision approaches in telomere-based cancer therapies.

In most body cells these caps shorten with every division, eventually limiting how long a cell can keep dividing. It is a natural brake on runaway growth."]},{"h":"How cancer escapes","p":["This review describes how cancer cells bypass that brake. They reactivate telomerase, an enzyme that rebuilds the caps, or use an alternative lengthening route, letting them divide unchecked and drive tumour growth."]},{"h":"Treatment possibilities","p":["The authors examine therapies aimed at telomerase and the alternative route, and how these systems interact with the cell's DNA repair machinery. They also flag real hurdles, including resistance and effects on healthy cells, arguing for precise, carefully targeted approaches."]}]}

posts.orig_sub: Targeting telomeres could stop tumors from dividing.

posts.credit: Nina Rembiałkowska, Katarzyna Rekiel, Piotr Urbanowicz, Mateusz Mamala, Karolina Marczuk, Maria Wojtaszek, Marta Żywica, Eivina Radzevičiūtė-Valčiukė, Vitalij Novickij, Julita Kulbacka · doi.org · open access
posts.title: How cancer tampers with the switches that control DNA
posts.sub: Drugs that reset these switches could help cells repair their DNA and fight tumours.
posts.author: Nina Rembiałkowska, Katarzyna Rekiel, Piotr Urbanowicz, Mateusz Mamala, Karolina Marczuk, Maria Wojtaszek, Marta Żywica, Eivina Radzevičiūtė-Valčiukė, Vitalij Novickij, Julita Kulbacka
posts.summary: Epigenetic modifications are heritable, reversible alterations that causally reshape chromatin architecture and thereby influence DNA repair without changing nucleotide sequence. DNA methylation, histone modifications and non-coding RNAs profoundly influence DNA repair mechanisms and genomic stability. Aberrant epigenetic patterns in cancer compromise DNA damage recognition and repair, therefore impairing homologous recombination (HR), non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), and base excision repair (BER) by suppressing key repair genes and lowering access to repair sites. Then it is dissected how loss-of-function mutations in Switch/Sucrose non-fermentable, imitation switch and CHD (Chromodomain helicase DNA-binding) chromatin-remodeling complexes impair nucleosome repositioning, preventing effective damage sensing and assembly of repair machinery. Non-coding RNAs contribute to epigenetic silencing at DNA break sites, exacerbating repair deficiencies. This review evaluates recent advances concerning epigenetic dysfunction and DNA repair impairment. It is also highlighted that nanoparticle-mediated delivery strategies are designed to overcome pharmacologic resistance.

With repair weakened, DNA damage accumulates, helping tumours grow and shrug off treatments."]},{"h":"Paths to treatment","p":["Because these changes are reversible, drugs that reset the switches could restore healthy gene control and repair. The authors also highlight delivery of such drugs in tiny particles, designed to overcome the resistance that limits current medicines."]}]}

posts.credit: Mark Louie D. Lopez, Ellika M. Crichton, Michael J. Allison, Anna H. Dema, Matthew T. Bonderud, Caren C. Helbing · doi.org · open access
posts.title: DNA tests for wildlife can survive storage and travel
posts.sub: Reliable, low-cost genetic surveys make it easier to track rare species in the field.
posts.author: Mark Louie D. Lopez, Ellika M. Crichton, Michael J. Allison, Anna H. Dema, Matthew T. Bonderud, Caren C. Helbing
posts.summary: Objective Environmental DNA (eDNA) detection is a transformative tool for ecological surveys which in many cases offers greater accuracy and cost-effectiveness for tracking low-density, cryptic species compared to conventional methods. For the use of targeted quantitative PCR (qPCR)-based eDNA detection, protocols typically require freshly prepared reagents for each sample, necessitating systematic evaluation of reagent stability within the functional context of eDNA standard curve preparation and environmental sample evaluation. Herein, we assessed the effects of long-term storage and freeze–thaw cycles on qPCR reagents for eDNA analysis across six assays. Results Results demonstrate qPCR plates (containing pre-made PCR mix, primer-probe, and DNA template) remain stable at 4 °C for three days before thermocycling without fidelity loss irrespective of qPCR assay used. Primer-probe mixes remain stable for five months of − 20 °C storage with monthly freeze-thaw cycles also irrespective of qPCR assay used. Synthetic DNA stocks maintain consistency in standard curves and sensitivity for three months under the same conditions.

That makes genetic monitoring of threatened species more practical and affordable."]}]}

posts.credit: Neha Acharya‐Patel, Mark Louie D. Lopez, Matthew T. Bonderud, Hajeong Lee, Emma T. Groenwold, Erin U. Foster, Linda M. Nichol, Caren C. Helbing · doi.org · open access
posts.title: Researchers detect sea otters from DNA left in seafloor mud
posts.sub: Reading genetic traces in mud could let scientists monitor threatened marine life without disturbing it.
posts.author: Neha Acharya‐Patel, Mark Louie D. Lopez, Matthew T. Bonderud, Hajeong Lee, Emma T. Groenwold, Erin U. Foster, Linda M. Nichol, Caren C. Helbing
posts.summary: Environmental DNA (eDNA) preserved in sediments (sed‐eDNA) holds promise for improving our understanding of historical species occurrences and contemporary biomonitoring. However, uneven DNA distribution, DNA fragmentation, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) inhibition present challenges to species detection. Herein, we evaluate the efficacy of sed‐eDNA methods to detect the presence of a patchily distributed marine mammal in a coastal marine ecosystem. We developed a targeted quantitative PCR (qPCR)‐based assay for the detection of sea otter ( Enhydra lutris ) DNA. This assay successfully amplified target DNA from aquaria occupied by sea otters and from two of eight seawater samples from areas where sea otters are often present. Additionally, we conducted an experiment to examine the utility of our assay in detecting sea otter DNA in sediment. We compared four sed‐eDNA extraction techniques and two DNA cleaning protocols in surface sediment samples taken from areas with varying sea otter occupancy. To test for DNA extraction efficiency, we used fish and chloroplast as endogenous controls.

posts.credit: Mark Louie D. Lopez, Ave Dersch, Paul Drevnick, Rute Clemente‐Carvalho, Evan Morien, Christopher F. G. Hebda, Erin Ussery, Mark E. McMaster, Matthew A. Lemay, Caren C. Helbing · doi.org · open access
posts.title: Lake mud confirms what Indigenous knowledge recorded
posts.sub: Genetic traces in sediment and traditional knowledge together tell a richer story of ecosystem change.
posts.author: Mark Louie D. Lopez, Ave Dersch, Paul Drevnick, Rute Clemente‐Carvalho, Evan Morien, Christopher F. G. Hebda, Erin Ussery, Mark E. McMaster, Matthew A. Lemay, Caren C. Helbing
posts.summary: Sedimentary DNA (sedDNA), a form of environmental DNA (eDNA) shed by aquatic organisms and preserved in sediment, is crucial for reconstructing historical community compositions in aquatic ecosystems. In Cowpar Lake (Dene name: Doghostú), Alberta, a significant landslide event in the early 1940s CE impacted the lake's geochemistry and fish populations, as documented by Indigenous Knowledge from the Chipewyan Prairie First Nation and corroborated by targeted fish sedDNA analyses. The present study used 18S rRNA and cytochrome oxidase I (COI) genes for DNA metabarcoding of a sediment core from Cowpar Lake to assess the effect of the documented landslide and to reconstruct the historical community composition of eukaryotic functional trophic groups, including photoautotrophs, mixotrophs, parasites, and consumers. Between 1948 and 1956 CE, a notable shift in community composition occurred, with a decline in the alpha diversity of eukaryotic amplicon sequence variants. The increased primary productivity and terrestrial organic input post‐1950 is correlated with an increased diversity of phototrophs and mixotrophs, suggesting potential algal blooms.

The genetic record matched the Indigenous account: fish DNA confirmed the landslide's impact, and a broader survey showed a clear shift in the lake's life between 1948 and 1956, with signs of algal blooms after 1950."]},{"h":"Why it matters","p":["Two independent records agreeing strengthens both of them. Pairing scientific tools with traditional knowledge gives a fuller picture of how ecosystems change over time, which can help guide restoration."]}]}

posts.credit: Mark Louie D. Lopez, Kate C. Rolheiser, Jacob Etzkorn, Jacob J. Imbery, Matthew A. Lemay, Iria Gimenez, Caren C. Helbing · doi.org · open access
posts.title: Acidifying seas change the DNA trails animals leave
posts.sub: Understanding this effect keeps genetic surveys of ocean life accurate as the seas change.
posts.author: Mark Louie D. Lopez, Kate C. Rolheiser, Jacob Etzkorn, Jacob J. Imbery, Matthew A. Lemay, Iria Gimenez, Caren C. Helbing
posts.summary: Anticipated future increases in CO 2 levels are predicted to have a diverse array of lethal and non‐lethal effects on the marine ecosystem. While there has been extensive research on the physiological impacts of ocean acidification on marine species, our understanding of how increasing levels of carbon dioxide affect the shedding and decay of environmental DNA and RNA (eDNA/eRNA) in marine habitats is limited. This may impede the effective adoption of environmental nucleic acid–based molecular tools for monitoring marine biodiversity and detecting rare or invasive species. In the present study, we conducted mesocosm experiments to determine the shedding and decay rate constants of eDNA and eRNA in M. gigas ( Magallana [ Crassostrea ] gigas ) using mitochondrially encoded tRNA leucine 1 ( mt‐tl1 ) marker at various partial pressures of CO 2 in seawater. To our knowledge, this is the first study manipulating seawater pH using CO 2 . We developed a sensitive and specific quantitative PCR‐based assay to detect M. gigas eDNA and eRNA. Higher CO 2 levels increased shedding rates, indicating greater organism stress and biological effects on oysters.
